A table for four in Studio City. Two legal pads.

body: The sun comes in through the Commons’ east windows for the first time since Monday and lands on every wet thing at once: the puddles on the patio, the chrome of the bike rack, the eucalyptus by the dish return, still dripping, each drop lit like a dropped coin on its way down. Half the tables have migrated outside in their coats. A boy in the omelet line is wearing sunglasses indoors, and nobody has the heart.

Jack got here at twenty past and held the table in the sun with the Carhartt and two forks laid crosswise, a Youngstown claim, and by now the claim has filled. Kevin has the clipboard, a blue ballpoint and a quiz face. Margot has a drop slip in front of her and a cup of hot water she hasn’t dressed with anything. And Theo is up before ten on a Friday, which hasn’t happened since the first week of September: Sigma Rho hasn’t let him sleep since Monday, and a gold pin the size of a thumbnail sits on the lapel of the blazer, and Hollis is retired and home in his teacup, and without an egg to be careful of, Theo has become insufferable in a new key.

The television over the cereal bar is on CNN with the sound off. The Mall in Washington is a field of knit hats and signs, and the chyron says MARCH FOR LIFE · WASHINGTON and nothing else. Doug Pruitt, passing under it with a tray of tater tots, stops and tilts his entire body toward the screen. “Dude. Is it this big tomorrow?”
Kevin doesn’t look up from the clipboard. “They’re saying thirty-five thousand. Smaller. Colder.”
“Than *that*?” Doug points a tot at the snow on the Mall.
“It’s the Embarcadero, Doug. The wind has a position.”
Doug lowers himself into the chair at the foot of the table with the tots and thinks about it, visibly. “Dude. Are you watching Conan tonight? It’s the last one.”
“I’m bringing popcorn,” Jack says.
“To where?”
“To a household.”
“He is smiling at a tater tot,” says Margot.
“As a brother —” Theo begins, to the butter.
“You’re a brother tomorrow night,” Jack says.
“I am a brother in my heart, Costigan. Tomorrow is paperwork.”
“What are you dropping?” Kevin asks Margot, because the slip is the kind of thing Kevin can’t leave face-up on a table.
“Organizational Behavior.” She signs the line and caps the pen, a vault door closing. “The syllabus said *synergize*. Page one, under learning outcomes.”
“That’s not grounds.”
“It is the only grounds there is, Kevin. The word is a confession. Also, I’m on the van tomorrow.”
The table looks at her. Doug, to whom the van has not been explained, looks at the table.
“It’s a pro-life march,” Kevin says.

“For science. Newman is my beat this semester, and a fifteen-passenger van is the only room in California a person can’t leave.” She drinks her hot water. “I cleared it with Peter. He asked whether I intended to pray. I said I intended to observe, and he said that was a start.”
“Bring a sandwich,” Kevin tells Jack. He taps the clipboard with the ballpoint. “Bring two. Peter’s stops are a matter of conscience.”

The list is a single sheet in Kevin’s blue hand, fourteen names in rows, and here and there one of them has been crossed out and written in again in pink marker, in a different hand. “Some people signed up late,” Kevin says, fast, and turns the sheet face-down against his chest. But Jack has already read it upside down, and BROUSSARD is on it. He knew it would be. He said yes anyway.

Before the eggs are cold he takes the RAZR out onto the patio, into the sun, and calls Gloria at home. She picks up on the first ring and says she has been up since five, so there is no waking her, whatever he’s done.
“I need Saturday off.”
“Is it the girl?”
“It’s a march.”
“Against what?”
“For.”
There is the sound of a kettle, and of a woman who has put her whole attention on a kettle in order to think. “Boysenberry going?”
“She doesn’t know yet.”

He lets that sit on the line. In the puddle at his boots the sky is intact, with a gull in it. “Rudy’s nephew has been after a Saturday since Thanksgiving,” Gloria says. “He gets this one.” And then, not unkindly: “That’s twice, hon.”

When he comes back in, the table has lost a Theo. Theo has taken his coffee to the next table over, “for the light,” where Laney is sitting alone with a tray, upright, lipsticked, the copper hair pinned up. The two of them are angled toward Jack at an exact and unconvincing angle. Jack looks at the sugar dispenser. Laney looks at the sugar dispenser. They have both settled on it.
“The thing people forget, Delaney,” Theo says, at the volume of a back row, “is that half of *communication* is the *ears*.”
“So true, Theodore.” Laney addresses her fruit cup. “You can’t know what someone’s *feeling* unless you *ask*.”
Jack looks up from his eggs, and they freeze: Theo with the cup halfway to his mouth, Laney with a strawberry on a fork, stopped in the air. Then they go on, worse.
“Ask, Theodore.”
“I’m *asking*, Delaney.”
“Then *listen*.”
“I’m *listening*.”
“Act two,” Margot says, without looking up from the drop slip. “They’ve been rehearsing.”

On the back of Jack’s chair, where he hung it at twenty past, is the pink umbrella he has had since yesterday afternoon, scalloped edge and brass handle. He lifts it off and holds it out across the gap between the tables, and Theo gets up and takes it by the middle, as if it were a flag from a coffin, and turns to the girl eighteen inches away.
“Delaney. Costigan returns the umbrella.”
Laney’s eyes stay on her tray. “Tell Costigan thank you.”
“She says thank you,” Theo says.
“I’m four feet away, Theo.”
Neither of them dignifies it. Laney stands, tray in both hands, chin level, and comes past Jack’s table on the way to the dish return, and says, at the temperature of the milk, “Costigan.”
She sets a granola bar down on his tray without a sound, carefully, as one sets something down near a man who might slam it, and says, “For the van,” and keeps her eyes on the dish return.

Kevin has turned the clipboard over again. Jack looks at the bar, and at the back of the copper head, and at the bar. In the fall she told him about Kaylee Whitmore on the Pi Lam steps at one in the morning, with a balloon on her wrist; since the week he got back from break she wouldn’t say his name in a room, or look at the part of it he was in. Since the basement she says it constantly, his last name and nothing after it, and then she leaves him a granola bar. He can’t make the three of her into one girl. He has stopped trying to guess which one is the act.

Theo comes back to Jack’s table alone and sits, as though none of it had occurred, and lifts his coffee to the light. “Listening, Costigan,” he says, as if the thought had just arrived. “It’s half of it.”

choices.text: “Is this about the birthday?”
response: “Everything is about the birthday,” Theo says. “The sheet cake has a subcommittee.” He reaches across and takes the second half of Jack’s toast, as tribute.
“I’m not on the subcommittee,” Kevin says.
“Nobody said you were, Tran. It hasn’t been formed. You are, however, under consideration.”

choices.text: “You two are being weird.”
response: “We’re being *supportive*,” Theo says. “Of each other. In public. It’s very modern.” He stirs a coffee that has never needed stirring, and Margot’s pen stays capped. Then, short, all the lacquer gone off it: “Eat your eggs, Costigan.”

choices.text: *Eat. Let him finish.*
response: Jack eats. Theo finishes, and the bit gets longer and worse: the ears, the heart, a thought he attributes to Truffaut that Truffaut did not have, a second movement on the subject of eye contact. It goes on until Kevin says, “He’s eating, Theo,” and Theo sits back, wounded, and steals a tot from Doug’s tray.

s03.slug: FRIDAY · 1:30 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE CURB → DEL PLAYA LANE, THE PORCH WITH NO SWING
body: The Saab is at the Delgado curb at one-thirty with the top down for the first time in a week, the canvas folded away behind the seats like a thing she’s finished with. Skye is behind the wheel in sunglasses, one arm laid along the door, her hair loose and her face turned up, doing nothing at all but sitting in a car in the sun.

Across Ocean Road the Commons has its big front window, and at a table in it, with a tray, Laney Price turns her head. She doesn’t turn it back. She watches the Saab, and the girl in it, and him coming across the wet grass toward both of them.
He sees her see it. He gets in.

She takes Ocean Road with one hand on the wheel and the other held up in the wind. “I’m solar,” she says. “Did you know that about me? I’ve been on a backup generator since Monday. Everything I said to you this week was the generator talking.” At the light at Las Olas she tips her head back against the seat and shuts her eyes behind the sunglasses with her face up, and the light goes green, and she stays like that, and the man in the pickup behind them leans on his horn, and she waves to him over her shoulder without opening her eyes.

On Del Playa the porch boards are steaming, the sun on the soaked wood lifting it off in a low white breath, and the house, which leans, leans into the light. Sol is on the top step in a man’s undershirt with a sheet of sandpaper, a long bleached limb of driftwood across her knees, sanding it toward something.
“What is it?” Jack says.
“Swing,” says Sol, and keeps sanding.

Over her head are the two hooks in the porch ceiling. Wednesday in the rain a length of chain still swung from one of them, tapping the post; now the chain is gone, and in the sun the bare hooks throw two small shadows on the boards, side by side.
*Oceanography 1* is drying on the porch rail, face down at chapter four, its pages rippled like something that has been to sea.

Through the screen door Tomás has a record on, a guitar coming up out of the dark of the front room bright and unhurried, and then Tomás himself comes to the screen, squints up at the blue over the street, which has been gone long enough to owe him an explanation, and says to Jack, “Maybe Sunday, bro.” He takes his head back inside.
Skye drops onto the step below Sol, takes the iced tea out of Sol’s hand, drinks half of it, and gives it back, and Sol accepts this as she accepts weather. Jack sits on the rail.
Jack tells her there. It has been in him since Kevin in the hall last night, and in the sun it has started to feel like something he’s keeping from her.
“I’m on a van tomorrow,” he says. “Five in the morning. The Walk for Life, in San Francisco.” She pushes her sunglasses up into her hair. “Kevin asked me. For him. He asked for himself.”
“Is all of Newman going?”
“It’s a Newman thing.”
Skye looks up at the hooks.
“That’s a yes, then,” she says. And then, fast, before he can get anything else into the air: “I’m coming.”
“It’s a pro-life march.”

“I know what it is. I read the news, Jack. I’m an informed corporation.” The sunglasses are back down. She’s talking quickly now. “I want to see what you believe in on the street. Not in a book, not in a pew — out in the road with thirty thousand people and their signs. I don’t have to believe it to watch you.”
“Do they let in people who aren’t —” She makes a gesture that takes in herself, her sunglasses, the Saab at the curb, the whole state of California.
“It’s a sidewalk, Skye.”
“I’ve been turned away from sidewalks.”
“The van leaves at five.”
“Five is a call time. Six is a choice.” She has it worked out already; she must have worked it out between *Newman* and *thing*. “I’ll drive up. I’ll find you at the part where they all talk first.”
“The rally.”

“I’ll find you at the rally.” And the next part is already loaded behind it. She’s sitting on the step below Sol with both arms locked around one knee and her chin up, braced, as she sat across from her mother and a legal pad at that lunch, with the answers ready to the things he hasn’t said yet: that people will look, that the van will talk, that Corinne will have a feeling about it.
He doesn’t make her get to the second answer.

choices.text: “I want you there.”
response: Her arms come off her knee. The braced thing goes out of her shoulders, all at once, like a coat let fall.
“Then I’m there,” she says.

She gets up, takes his hand off the porch rail, and walks him in by it — through the screen door, past Tomás on the arm of the couch with his eyes shut, conducting, past the record turning in the dark — and up the stairs, which are too narrow for two people holding hands, and she doesn’t let go of it on the stairs either.

choices.text: “Don’t bring a sign. They’re heavier than they look.”
response: “I’m bringing coffee,” she says. “Coffee’s lighter.”

She’s up and backing through the screen door ahead of him, still arguing about the sign she isn’t bringing — what it would say, what font, whether a sign that just said HI on a stick would get her killed or elected — and she argues it up the stairs backward, one step above him, which puts her mouth exactly level with his, and she knows it, and keeps arguing.

choices.text: “Some of it’s going to be hard to look at. For you.”
response: “Then I’ll look at you,” she says.
She says it lightly, and doesn’t take it back. On the top step Sol stops sanding. Sol starts again.

Skye stands and holds the screen door open with her hip, and goes in ahead of him and up the stairs into the dark of the house with one hand trailing behind her on the rail, low, where he can reach it.

s04.slug: FRIDAY · 2:30 PM · DEL PLAYA LANE, HER ROOM — DAYLIGHT
body: He has only ever been in this room at night. Now the window over the mattress is open on the Channel, and the Channel is bright as tin all the way out to the islands, and the surf comes up through the window loud after six days of storm, so loud they would have to raise their voices to fight. On the wall over the dresser the sun has laid down a square of itself, the shape of the window, sharp at the edges and a little crooked, on the old plaster.
Skye reaches past him for the cord of the blind.

It’s an old roll-up blind gone the color of weak tea, and he has never seen it down. There has never been anything in here to keep out. Her hand is on the cord, and her eyes are on the cord and not on him, and he has never seen her do that either.
He puts his hand over hers on the cord and leaves it there — not pulling, not anything. She looks at him for a long moment. Then she lets go of the cord herself. The blind stays up.
“It’s very bright,” she says.
“It’s the sun.”
“I’ve heard of it.” She takes her hand back from under his and puts it on his face instead, and turns it to the window, so the light is on him first. “I just never got a good look at you in it.”
“*That one most*,” she says against his ear, in his own words, which she seems to have been carrying around in her pocket all week.
After that there’s nothing to argue with but the daylight.

In the dark there was always somewhere for his face to go. Under the lamp there was a circle and a room beyond it, and the room was a kind of privacy. Here there is no beyond. The sun is on the sheets and on her shoulders and down the long line of her to her heels, and it’s on him, all of him, and there is nowhere in this room that isn’t lit, and nothing either of them does in it will be able to pass itself off as a dream afterward. The wind comes in off the water and raises the gooseflesh along her arms and he puts his mouth there and watches it go down again. Her skin is warm on the side the sun has been on and cool on the other, and he finds the line where one turns into the other with his hand, and follows it, and she shivers and laughs and tells him he’s doing geography. He wants her. He has wanted her since a window seat in Montecito, and in this light the wanting has nowhere to hide either, and he doesn’t ask it to.

Where every time before now one of them has stopped, she stops. She doesn’t move away; she only goes still, her hand flat and warm low on his stomach, and lets him feel her waiting, and he knows what she’s waiting for, because he has always said it here, and it has always held. He opens his mouth to say it. What comes out instead is lower, into her hair, half of it need and half of it a shame that climbs all the way up his face in the sun.
“Not that.” His hand closes over her wrist and keeps it where it is. “But anything else you want.”

She lifts her head to look at him. For a second her face has nothing ready on it, and then a grin comes up across it, slow and entirely without mercy, the kind no director ever got out of her on purpose.
“Anything,” she says, trying the word out. She folds her arms on his chest and sets her chin on them, a woman with all afternoon and the best seat in the house. “Only if you tell me out loud first.”

So he tells her. He does it badly. There is no voice to do it in, no bit, nothing he has ever said in a dorm or a confessional or a car that is any use to him now, and the sun is on his face the whole time with nowhere for it to go. He starts with the easy one: he wants the shirt off her, here, with the blind up, because he has never once seen all of her in the light. She sits up and pulls it over her head and drops it on the floor and waits, bare to the waist in the square of sun, and says, *Go on*. So he goes on. He wants her hand on him, he says to the ceiling, and not the way it’s been in the dark, quick and half-dressed, as if they were stealing it. She takes his chin and turns his face back to hers. He wants her mouth, he says then, and the word comes out of him at about the volume of a confession, and his ears go hot to the tips. And he wants — he loses the end of the sentence and just says *you*, and she laughs right in his face and asks him to be more specific, wide-eyed, a schoolteacher. So he is. He wants to put his mouth on her, he says. All the way down. He wants to find out what she sounds like when she isn’t doing a voice. He hears himself say every word of it in the full light of a Friday afternoon, and something in him that has been keeping count all year sits down and puts its head in its hands.

When he runs out, she doesn’t say anything at first. She looks down at him, and under the delight there is something she isn’t playing for anybody, as if he has handed her a thing nobody ever thought to hand her: not a favor, not a callback — just what he wants. Then she’s back in character, low, against his mouth. “See? You *can* ask for things.”

And this time they don’t stop at the edge of it. She undresses him herself, the belt and then the rest, slowly, making him lie still for it, and then she sheds what’s left of her own and kneels over him in the sun with nothing on but the little silver anklet, and lets him look as long as he wants, which is a long time. Her hand first. She takes him in her hand and watches his face while she does it, unhurried, learning what makes his breath catch and doing that again on purpose, and when he’s shaking she bends her head and takes him in her mouth, and he says her name to the ceiling like a man falling off something. She doesn’t let him look away. She keeps her eyes up on his the whole time, in the full sun, and there’s no joke he can get to and no dark to turn his face into, and when he comes it goes through all of him at once, his hand knotted in the sheet and the other in her hair, and her name comes out of him like something he’s dropped and can’t pick up. Afterward she lays her cheek on his stomach and laughs, low and pleased with herself, and he can feel the laugh more than hear it.

Then it’s his turn, and he takes his time about it, because she did. He kisses his way down her, her throat and the hollow under it and her breasts, warm on the sunlit side and cool on the other, down the soft skin of her stomach, and she watches him go with her lip in her teeth, and when he gets where he’s going she says, “Oh,” and nothing else for a while. He has never done this. She can tell, and she doesn’t pretend she can’t; she puts her hand in his hair and shows him, *there*, *slower*, *no — there*, and then she stops directing and her hips come up off the mattress and her heel digs into his back, and he learns what her face does when it has stopped performing for anyone. Her laugh breaks in the middle and turns into something that isn’t a laugh. Her hand grips the back of his head. She says his name to the ceiling, and then again, the second time like an argument she has decided to lose, and she comes against his mouth shaking, loud, not caring who on Del Playa has a window open. Somewhere in the middle of it the mattress, which lives on the floor and has never had a frame, travels most of a foot toward the wall, and afterward they both lift their heads to look at how far it went, and she says, “Sol’s going to hear about that,” and he says Sol already did. Downstairs Tomás’s record goes on to the next song, discreetly, like a waiter leaving a room.

Later she props herself on an elbow in the sun from the window, her hair falling forward over one shoulder, and looks down at him. Over the dresser the square of light has slid a hand’s width down the wall.
“So what’s the difference now?” she says.

Her voice is the one from the Lagoon path, the walk-and-explain voice, lying down. “After that? Tell me the difference between that and the thing.” She puts one finger in the middle of his chest, not to push. “Because every time I find your line, it’s somewhere else. It was a shirt once. Then it was my underwear. Last Saturday there wasn’t anything left of it but a word.” The finger taps, once. “And today it’s *not that*, and then a list. Show me where *that* is. I’m not trying to get you to. I’m asking. I want to understand it.”
He goes looking for it.

There has always been one. He comes from a kitchen where people argue the line between a mortal sin and a venial one over the dishes, and he has always had the distinction ready, the word for what’s allowed and the word for what isn’t, a fence he could show her. He goes to where the fence should be, and there isn’t one. Not for this. Augustine prayed to be made chaste, *but not yet*, and Jack has always found that line funny, and he isn’t laughing. He isn’t going to lie on her mattress in the sun and tell her that what they just did was nothing. He knows what it was. He knew at the door, and on the stairs, and with *anything else* in his mouth, and he’ll know in the coat closet at St. Brendan’s, saying all of it a second time, to a man behind a linen screen. And he isn’t going to tell her the one thing is different in some way he could draw for her, because he can’t draw it, and she would see through it inside a minute. The one thing is the one thing he isn’t going to do without a promise. He can’t make that true by explaining it. He opens his mouth and there is nothing ready in it at all.

She has watched him lose arguments, to her, gladly, under a dead umbrella. She has never seen him without one. It shows on her face — interest first, and then something quicker, and less sure of itself.
She comes up nearer on her elbow, her hair falling on his chest, and starts to ask it again, lower.

choices.text: *Tell her the truth: there isn’t a difference you can explain. It’s still no.*
choices.key: In daylight Skye asked you the difference, and you told her you didn’t have one — and kept the no.
response: He tells her the truth, in the light, because it’s the only thing in the room he can’t be caught out in, and because she asked him to know, not to win.

That he went looking for the difference and it isn’t there. That he’s not going to tell her what they just did was nothing, because it wasn’t nothing — not to him, and not, he’s fairly sure, to God, and she can laugh at that part if she wants to. She doesn’t. And that he’s not going to tell her the one thing is different because of some rule he can recite, because he could recite it, and she’d hear him reciting.
She listens with her chin on his breastbone and her eyes on his. When he stops there’s nothing but the surf through the window.
“So what is it, then?” she says. “If it isn’t a difference.” She isn’t teasing. She has her hand over his heart, feeling for the answer through the bone.
He gives her the only true thing he has left.
“I don’t have an argument. I have a no.”

choices.text: *Let it go to the very edge before you say it.*
choices.key: In daylight you let it go to the very edge before you said it — and kept the no.
response: He doesn’t answer her. She stops asking with words, and he lets her ask the other way, and lets it come.

He lets it come all the way. To the edge of the thing she’s asking about and then the last of the edge, the place where answering and not answering are the same breath, where nothing has happened yet and everything is about to, close to the width of a word — her eyes open on his, the sun on both their faces, the surf loud below the window. He has never let it come this far. Her breath has stopped. Her fingers have gone still on the back of his neck.

Her mouth is open against his. Her heart is going so hard he can feel it in his own chest, and his in hers, and neither rhythm is his to choose anymore. Nothing has happened that can’t be stopped. Stopping is all it is. It takes everything he has, and then it takes a little more than that, from somewhere he didn’t know he was keeping anything.
He stops. He says it against her mouth, hoarse, with no breath left over to say it with.
“I don’t have an argument. I have a no.”
choices.cue: Skye felt how close it was.

choices.text: *Hold her and give her the one reason you have, badly.*
choices.key: In daylight you held Skye and gave her the one reason you have, badly — and kept the no.
response: He gets his arms around her and pulls her down against him, her cheek on his collarbone, and holds on, and tries.

It’s the one thing he’d be promising with, he tells her. Everything else they do, he does knowing what it is, and he’ll answer for it, and he keeps doing it anyway, apparently — that part comes out wrong. But the one thing is a promise. It’s the body saying *for good*, and he can’t say for good yet; he’s eighteen, he’s — It comes out worse than that, all of it, in pieces, with the surf louder than he is, and he knows how bad it sounds before each piece is out.

He says something about his mother and stops. He says something about promises that comes out sounding like the inside of a greeting card, and stops again. She lets him get through every piece. She doesn’t help him. When he runs out she lifts her head off his collarbone to look at him, close, with the sun in her eyelashes.
He gives up on the reasons and gives her what’s under them.
“I don’t have an argument. I have a no.”

s04a.slug: FRIDAY · 3:50 PM · DEL PLAYA LANE, HER ROOM — THE LIGHT ON THE WALL
body: Skye laughs.

It comes up out of her into his shoulder, helpless — at him, because he lost, because he had nothing left and said no anyway, as if no were a thing you could just have — and she laughs until the mattress shakes and her hair is in both their mouths.

“You lost,” she says, into the shoulder. “You lost, and you won anyway. By forfeit. You can’t win by forfeit, there are *rules* —” She can’t get the rest out. She comes up for air and tries again. “That,” she says, “is the most annoying thing anyone has ever done to me in daylight.”

She lifts her head. Her eyes are wet from it, and her face is pink to the hairline, and she looks at him from very close, memorizing something. She doesn’t argue it any further. She kisses him instead, slowly, and doesn’t stop.

She keeps the no exactly where he put it. The one thing is out of the room and nothing else is, and the afternoon doesn’t cool by a degree. She pulls him down onto her, skin to skin from mouth to knee, and they go at each other in the full light as long and as near as it can go without crossing: his hand between her thighs and hers wrapped around him, both of them moving against each other on the bare mattress, her heel hooked behind his knee, the sweat cooling on the small of her back in the wind from the window and coming again. Twice it comes right up against the line, so close he can feel exactly where it is, and both times she stops there, precisely, her eyes open on his, and waits until he knows where they are, and then laughs low in her throat and starts again from somewhere else — her mouth on his chest, her hand slow and then not slow, his name in his ear in a voice he has never heard on any television. She brings him off a second time with her hand and her eyes on his face, and he brings her off with his fingers while she bites his shoulder to keep from waking the street, and nobody in the room pretends not to be looking. Over the dresser the square of sun slides down the wall a little at a time, across the drawer pulls and the mirror and down toward the corner, the clock of the whole afternoon, and they let it go where it’s going. Downstairs the record runs out and stays out.

When it has nearly reached the corner she’s on her side with her head on his arm, watching it. Her face in the sun has nothing on it, not even the sunglasses: a crease from the pillow down one cheek, a little burn across her nose from the drive with the top down, her eyelashes pale at the tips where the light comes through them. He has seen this face on Gloria’s Zenith at the Anchor with every hair put where somebody wanted it. He has never seen it like this, in the afternoon, with no one deciding anything about it.
“Every time anybody’s seen me in daylight,” she says, “there was a crew.”
The square is nearly at the floor.
“Somebody with a meter at my face. Somebody who knew where the sun was going to be.” She watches it. “I never had to look.”
He doesn’t answer her. He reaches down for the sheet and brings it up over the two of them, as far as her shoulders and no farther, so the sun is still on her face.
The square slides into the corner and thins to a bar, and the bar goes off the wall, and the room is just a room in the late afternoon, with the window open and the sea in it.

s05.slug: FRIDAY · 5:20 PM · DEL PLAYA LANE, THE FRONT ROOM — HOPE FOR HAITI NOW
body: Tomás’s television hums before it shows anything — a thin high whine from somewhere deep in its back — and then the picture swims up out of the dark a little green. It has been green since whoever left a rear-projection set the size of a refrigerator in this house left it. Tomás goes through six channels with the remote to prove a point he never states, and it’s the same stage on all six. Candles. A long dark room. Sol and Tomás are on the couch with a mixing bowl of tortilla chips in the middle cushion, and Jack is on the floor with his back against the couch, and Skye is beside him on the floor with her knees up, in one of his shirts and nothing much else.

George Clooney is at the front of it in Los Angeles in a dark suit, being grave, which suits him. Behind him are long tables of famous people in headsets answering telephones — a man from a sitcom, a singer, an actor Jack’s mother would know, writing down credit card numbers with their heads bent like people taking an exam. Wyclef is in New York. A man with a guitar Jack would know anywhere stands alone in a spotlight and sings something old and slow, and the couch is quiet through all of it.
Skye has gone quiet — the quiet she does in a full room.
“Nobody called me,” she says.
Sol looks over. Skye has her eyes on the screen.

“It’s not a complaint. That’s how it works.” She points with a chip at the long tables, and her voice is a professional’s, level, a woman going over somebody else’s books. “They asked people with movies. You get a phone if you’ve got something opening in the spring, or if you need the spring to forget something. That one’s opening. That one’s forgetting. Somebody’s publicist made a call for every chair in that room, and Corinne could tell you which by now.” She eats the chip. “And it works. You’ll tell your friends George Clooney took your Visa, and you’ll give twice what you meant to. It’s a little disgusting and it works, and I’d do it in a second. Five years ago they’d have put me at the end of a table in a cardigan, between a soap and a kid from a cereal ad, and I’d have been thrilled.”

Then she sits up straight and puts an imaginary headset on, and becomes the girl at the end of the table, radiant, sincere, one finger to her ear. “Hi! It’s a person from a show you’ve heard of. How much do you love Haiti?” A nod, enormous. “That’s *so* much. Can you love it more?”
Tomás laughs through his nose. Sol doesn’t, and looks at Skye. Skye takes her finger down from her ear and puts her hand back in the chip bowl, and leaves it there without taking one.

He doesn’t try to fix it. There’s a number running along the bottom of the screen in white, under the candles, and he reads it to her, slowly, every digit, the way Ma reads a phone number to Nonna, so she has it.

Skye looks at him. She gets her white phone out of the shirt pocket and turns it over, and from a slot in the back of the case she slides a black card he has never seen, plain. Skylark’s, he guesses; the accountant in Encino’s.
She dials. He says it from the floor: “Corporations have no consciences.”
“Skylark does tonight,” says Skye, with the phone at her ear.

Somebody answers, a long way off, and she says good evening and thanks them for being there so late. She spells it for the volunteer. *S-K-Y-L-A-R-K.* Pictures. Inc. Like the bird, yes. She reads the card number off the black card in a clear voice with her hair in her face, and the expiration date, and the zip code in Encino, and then the volunteer must ask her how much, because she says, flat, as a fact: “Twenty-five thousand dollars.”

Jack watches her give it away with the phone tucked against her shoulder, reading numbers to a stranger in a room full of famous people who didn’t call her, and he couldn’t look anywhere else if the house came down around them.
She thanks the volunteer. She hangs up.
Without a word, Tomás leans down off the couch and sets the bowl of tortilla chips in her lap.
On the screen the man with the guitar has finished, and the room in Los Angeles is applauding in the dark, and Sol reaches for the remote and turns it up.

s06.slug: FRIDAY · 11:35 PM · DEL PLAYA LANE, THE FRONT ROOM — CONAN’S LAST SHOW
body: By eleven-thirty-five the front room is lit by the television and nothing else, green and blue and moving on all of their faces, and the pop Jack brought is going flat on the floor in four mismatched glasses.
She made the popcorn, as promised, in the biggest mixing bowl in the house, and puts it in his lap, and he holds it.

Sol and Tomás are on the floor in front of the couch, Sol with her back against Tomás’s knees and a blanket around both of them, and Jack and Skye have the couch, and the couch has a spring in the middle that has opinions. Conan comes out to an ovation that won’t stop. The monologue is about NBC, all of it, and the audience laughs loudest at the jokes about the building they’re sitting in. Tom Hanks comes on and is kind. Neil Young comes on and plays, and Tomás sits up straight for him, reverently, a man in church.

Skye watches with her feet tucked under her and a fistful of popcorn she forgets to eat. “Look at his hands,” she says, about Conan. “Look. He doesn’t know where to put them. Sixteen years and he still doesn’t know where to put his hands.” She says it like good news about an old friend.

At the end Will Ferrell comes out in a long blond wig with a cowbell, and the band comes in behind him, and Beck and Ben Harper and Billy Gibbons, and it’s “Free Bird,” the whole thing, the full long ridiculous run of it, and Tomás is on his feet in the blue light playing every note of it on an air guitar with his eyes shut, and Sol is laughing silently into the blanket, and Skye is keeping time on the side of the popcorn bowl with a fingernail, cowbell for cowbell.

Then Conan is at the front of it, alone, with the band quiet behind him, and he says goodbye. He thanks everybody. He says — Jack gets it only as an idea, as he gets most homilies — that he hates cynicism, that it doesn’t lead anywhere; that if you work hard and you’re kind, things turn out better than you thought. He says it fast, and for once his hands are still.
Skye has stopped laughing.

“When I was fourteen,” she says, to the screen, “my mother rented a two-bedroom in Studio City. For the commute. The lot was eleven minutes away. She timed it.” Her voice is ordinary. “There was a TV on the dresser at the end of my bed, the size of a lunchbox. I had a six o’clock call most days and I could not sleep. I could never sleep. And at twelve thirty-five he came on, from New York, on this little set at the end of the bed, with the sound way down so she wouldn’t hear it through the wall —” She stops. “He was the only person on television who looked as scared as I was. Every night. Like he’d just been told he was on. And he did it anyway.”
On the screen the band has started up again, and people are crying in the audience, and Conan is shaking hands.

“I used to do the monologue with him,” Skye says. “Under the covers. I knew the rhythm before I knew any of the jokes.” And then she’s crying, and he doesn’t think it’s for Conan, who is fine, who is rich and settled and saw to his staff. He thinks it’s for the girl at the end of the bed in Studio City, with the sound down so her mother wouldn’t hear, running lines with a man in New York at a quarter to one in the morning because there was nobody in the apartment to run them with.

Jack puts the bowl down on the floor, and she doesn’t ask him to. He puts his hand on her back, between her shoulder blades, where she carries the bad nights, and keeps it there. She leans back into it. Sol, on the floor, reaches up without turning around and holds Skye’s ankle a minute, and lets go.

At ten to one Skye walks him to the door. He has an alarm set for four-thirty and she knows it; she has said so twice, in two voices, and the second one was Gloria’s. On the porch in the dark she straightens the collar of the Carhartt with both hands, as if she’s sending him to school.
“Go be holy,” she says.

He walks home up Del Playa with his hands in his pockets and the cold coming off the water. The street has dried in the sun and gone damp again in the dark, and the eucalyptus at the top of the lane are dripping their menthol onto the sidewalk.

The van leaves at five. At three-thirty tomorrow afternoon, when Osei opens the closet door at St. Brendan’s, he’ll be in San Francisco. *Next Saturday,* Osei said. *Whatever you bring.* He’s bringing more than he had.

And he is happy. He can feel it in his legs. He knows to the dollar what it costs, and he’s happy anyway, and both of those are true at once, on the same street, and neither one is going to talk the other out of it tonight.

At the top of the lane he stops and looks back down it, past the dark houses, to the Channel. Half a moon is going down into the water to the west, white, sharp-edged as something cut with scissors, the first moon anybody in Marisol has seen in a week.

The alarm Jack set for 4:30 has been dead for eight minutes, and the room is still black, the window a slightly less black square in it. He is sitting on the edge of the bed in the Mooney hoodie, lacing his boots by feel, after three hours and ten minutes of something that was not quite sleep.

Across the room, a shape sits up against the dark: the wine-colored robe, the knees together, the hands on them. On the nightstand the teacup has caught the hall light under the door, with the retired egg in it. Theo has not been woken. Theo, by the posture, has been waiting.

“Item,” Theo says. “Sandwich at hour four, not hour two. Item. The cooler is not furniture. Item. Whatever Peter tells you about the route, he is wrong by eleven minutes, and he will tell you with love. Item.” A pause, and the pitch goes out of his voice, and what is left is short. “Take the window, Costigan. The aisle is for people who want to leave.”
Jack, one boot on: “What?”
Theo doesn’t say it again. He sits in the dark with his hands on his knees, having delivered the line, and the line stays delivered.
Then, too gently for Theo, to the dark: “A man who’s hurt should sit where the light is.” Jack doesn’t answer it. He ties the second boot.

He gets up and finds the Carhartt on the chair, and the two sandwiches in the Ziploc that he built at one in the morning on the desk with a plastic knife, and goes for the door. Behind him a pen cap clicks, a pad tears, a robe moves. Theo is there before the door is open, a feat before noon in the five months Jack has known him, and holds it for him with one hand and claps him on the back with the other, once, flat.
“Godspeed, Father Jack.”
On the stairs, between three and two, he shrugs the jacket straight on his shoulders and something crackles at his back. He reaches around and comes away with a square of yellow paper.

body.title: A Post-it, on the back of his jacket
body.text: WINDOW.

body: The lobby doors carry a new laminate, taped dead center at eye height, in Priya’s capitals.

body.title: Priya’s laminate, on the lobby door
body.text:
VAN PEOPLE: QUIET.
THE REST OF US: ASLEEP.

body: He pushes through it into the cold. The stars are still up over the Grove, more of them than the sodium lights usually allow.

s08.slug: SATURDAY · 4:55 AM · ST. BRENDAN’S LOT — THE NEWMAN VAN
body: The Newman van sits under the one sodium light in St. Brendan’s lot with its side door rolled open, a white fifteen-passenger Ford with ST. BRENDAN THE NAVIGATOR lettered small on the driver’s door, and the light turns everybody standing around it the same flat orange and their breath the same gold. Ocean Road is empty in both directions. Down the hill, in the dark, the surf is loud.

Peter Haddad is already behind the wheel with a steel thermos between his knees and a laminated route taped to the dash, going down it with one finger, his lips moving. Kenzie Rourke has the passenger seat and a road atlas open across her lap to a page she won’t need. Tyler Brandt and Bridget McNulty are feeding the back of the van a stack of signs on sticks, face down, so the words don’t show. Becca Lindell, in a long knitted scarf that goes around her twice, sees him crossing the lot and waves with her whole arm. Clare Dominguez is standing guard over a backpack with more sticks poking out of the top of it. Margot, in black to the chin, lifts her own thermos at him from the curb stop.
“For science,” she says, as if he’d asked.
“COSTIGAN,” says Joey Abruzzo, at a volume meant for a stadium, and up behind the church a rectory window lights and goes dark again.
“Joey Abruzzo.” It comes from the side door, quick and low and pure Mid-City. “It is five in the morning and Father is asleep forty feet from your mouth. The Lord can hear you at half.”

Kevin comes around the back of the van with a clipboard under one arm and sees him and stops. “You came,” he says, and nothing fast comes after it. He stands there in the orange light, and then he remembers he has a clipboard.

Jack takes the backpack of signs off Clare, who says it’s fine, it’s fine, they’re heavier than they look, and lets him, and he swings it up into the van for her. Becca hugs him around the neck in passing, scarf and all, and says, “You came! Kevin said you would and I said I’d believe it at five,” and it is five, and she lets him go.

Lena is at the open side door with the sign-up against her chest. She ran it; that’s her handwriting down every line. She’s in the gray cardigan under a navy peacoat buttoned to the throat, her hair twisted up off her neck, a pen in her other hand. She checks Clare off with a hand on her arm, and Becca with a “Morning, Becca,” warm and low, and then she finds his name and ticks it without looking up.
“Costigan.”
The pen goes on to the next line.

Kevin reads the seats off his own list. It’s the sheet from the Commons, in rows, in Kevin’s careful blue hand, with the pink in it. “Row one, Haddad, Rourke. Row two, Tran, Dominguez.” He clears his throat at nothing. “Row three. Costigan. Broussard.”
Everybody goes quiet in the way of a lot of people not looking. Bridget stops with a sign halfway into the van. Even Joey stops.
“It’s alphabetical,” Kevin says.
“We’re not next to each other alphabetically.”
“By first name.”
Jack looks at the list in Kevin’s hand, at the two names on the pink line. “Jack and Lena?”
Kevin’s ears go dark red under the sodium light. “…It’s a system.”

Row three is a bench for three. The aisle end of it is already taken by the big red cooler and Clare’s backpack of signs, side by side, with the seat belt pulled across both. “Cargo,” Kevin says. “It’s in the system.”
Jack doesn’t ask to move. At the side door Lena slides the clipboard under her arm and doesn’t ask either. Whoever asks first is the one who asked.

choices.text: *Take the window, like Theo said.*
response: He climbs in past the cooler and takes the window. Somewhere in the Carhartt is a square of yellow paper that says so.

Lena gets in last, after she has counted heads twice and slid the side door shut on the cold. She takes the middle, against the cooler, with the clipboard on her knees, and settles her peacoat under her, and looks straight ahead at the back of Kevin’s head.

choices.text: *Give her the window.*
response: He stands back by the cooler and lets the row be hers.

Lena looks at the window, and at him. Then she gets in past him without a word and takes it, and folds her peacoat under her, and puts the clipboard on her knees. He takes the middle. The cooler is against his right knee, cold through the denim, for the next three hundred miles.

choices.text: “Is there a mechanism for appeal?”
response: “There’s no mechanism,” Kevin says, instantly. “I checked.”
Somebody in the back laughs, and Becca says, “Oh, *Kevin*,” fondly, and Kevin looks down at the list, betrayed, and reads it out again: Costigan, middle; Broussard, window.
Lena gets in and takes the window. Jack gets in after her and takes what the system has left him. From his knee to hers there are six inches of gray vinyl, and then on his other side the cooler.

s09.slug: SATURDAY · 5:20 AM · US-101 NORTH, GAVIOTA → PASO ROBLES — ROW THREE
body: Peter takes the van up the coast in the dark with both hands on the wheel, and off to the left the Channel is black, with one oil platform lit far out on it. The dome lights are off. The heater is on high and smells of wet wool. In the rows behind, the people who got up at four are going back under one at a time — heads against the glass, against each other, against Becca’s scarf. In row two Clare is asleep against the window with a rosary in her lap and Kevin is pretending not to be asleep beside her.

The only reading light lit in the van is the one over row three, and it’s hers: a small hard cone of yellow on the clipboard on her knees, where she is going down the sign-up again in her small upright hand, and then a second page, the Haiti money, a column of figures she totals with the pen moving and her lips still.

body.text: He has the window, cold against his shoulder. The light falls on her hands and on the edge of his sleeve.
She has the window; he has the middle. The light falls on her hands and on his knee.

body: Where the freeway runs along the water she looks up from the column, at the little lamp over their heads, and then at him.
“Is the light going to bother you?”
“No.”
“Tell me if it does.”
“I will.”

It is perfectly polite. He would rather she had hit him with the clipboard. In the fall she did her figures out loud at him over a Commons tray and made him check her carrying, and argued when he was right. Now she totals by herself, under her own light, and asks after his comfort, and goes back to the page.

At Gaviota the coast turns away and the hills close in black on both sides, and the van goes into the tunnel and the sound of everything changes, a long hollow roar like the inside of a shell. Peter says over his shoulder, into the dark, “Okay. Before sunrise. Lena, would you?”
“The first Joyful Mystery,” Lena says. “The Annunciation.”
A girl in a back room in a town with no reputation, and an angel with a question. Nonna used to say it was the one time in Scripture that God asked and then waited for the answer.

She leads it low and quick and exact, the Our Father and then the Hail Marys, and the van comes in under her half asleep, a mumble from the back rows like a six-thirty Mass in February, and the tunnel lets them out the far side into the pass.

On the fourth Hail Mary, Margot, from row four, comes in on *Holy Mary, Mother of God* while Lena is still on *the fruit of thy womb*, hears it, and, for science, keeps going. She finishes the second half a clause ahead of the van, alone, with total confidence. Lena doesn’t stop. The rest of the van catches up with Margot at *sinners*.

Jack says it with them, at the speed of the van, with his hands between his knees. He doesn’t make any of the words smaller than they are. *Pray for us sinners* — there’s a way to say that line so it slides by, like a car doing exactly the limit past a cruiser, and his mother would hear it from the kitchen; there’s a way to drop it altogether, and Nonna would hear that from her chair in her sleep. Yesterday is all through him, the sun on the wall, every bit of it, and the line goes straight there and lands. He says it anyway, every time it comes around. It was true before he got in the van. And this morning he needs it said over him by somebody, and the van will do. The van says it ten times.

On the Glory Be, Lena’s free hand goes up to her collar, to the place under the peacoat where the medal is, and holds it through the wool — *as it was in the beginning* — and comes back down to the clipboard on *amen*. In the dark it’s the one thing he can see her do.
“Thank you, Lena,” Peter says. “Tyler, the second.”

Tyler takes the second and Bridget the third, and somewhere in the fourth the back rows go under for good, and by the end of the fifth the only voices answering are Peter’s and Kenzie’s and Lena’s and his. Peter says the Hail Holy Queen alone, and then it’s quiet. That’s the rule. The rosary, then quiet.

In the quiet he can hear her pen. He can hear the tires change their note on a bridge, and a semi going by the other way with a long sigh of air brakes, and somebody in the back row breathing slow and deep through the nose. Lena doesn’t sleep. Her pen stops for long stretches and starts again. Once her head goes back against the seat and her eyes close, and he holds very still, so as not to be the thing that moves, and after a minute the pen starts again.
South of Santa Maria the strawberry fields start, both sides of the freeway, mile on mile of plastic over the rows, pale in the dark, like furniture under dust sheets in a shut-up house.

Kevin passes the coffee back from row two in a tower of Dixie cups, out of a gas-station carafe he filled at half past four, and it is a crime: thin, scorched, the temperature of old bathwater. Jack drinks half of his to be polite and holds the rest.
Lena tastes hers and leans forward to the seat back, low, so as not to wake anybody. “Kevin Tran. I love you like a brother, and this coffee is a sin against the Fifth Commandment.”
“It’s from the Chevron,” Kevin whispers.
“I know where it’s from. I can taste the pumps.”

She sits back. Beside him, in the cone of light, she unscrews the cap of her own thermos — a dented green Stanley, older than both of them, somebody’s father’s — and pours, and the smell comes across the bench, real coffee, with chicory in it. She holds the cap out to him without a word, still reading the sign-up.

He takes it. She has it by the very rim, so he has to take it by the bottom, and the coffee shivers in it with the road, and at sixty miles an hour it takes some doing, on her part and on his, for no part of one hand to touch any part of the other. They manage it. There’s a chip out of the rim on one side, a little half-moon of bare steel, and he drinks from the other side. It’s very good coffee. When it’s empty he gives the cap back the same careful way, and she fills it for herself, and drinks from the chipped side.

North of San Luis Obispo the road climbs the Cuesta Grade in long curves, and on the first one the van leans and her knee comes against his, and on the next one it’s still there. He doesn’t move his. He can feel the seam of her jeans through his own, and the warmth of her through both, and he sits with it to the top of the grade with his eyes front and his coffee hand very still. She doesn’t move hers either. At the summit the road straightens and she shifts on the bench to reach her pen, and it’s gone, and the place on his knee goes on knowing where it was.

Past Atascadero the dark thins out over the hills to the east, and goes gray, and then goes to no color at all, and Kenzie wakes up in the front seat long enough to say “Oh, it’s morning,” as if it had been her idea, and at Paso Robles the vineyards come up out of the frost on both sides of the freeway: rows and rows of bare black vines on their wires, cut back hard to the knuckle, white on the ground in the alleys, and men walking down the rows in the first light in hooded sweatshirts and work gloves, bent over, with shears, pruning. Their breath goes up. One of them straightens at the end of a row with a hand at the small of his back and looks at the road. They don’t stop for the van. They’ve got the valley to get through before the sap comes up.
Lena has stopped totaling. The pen is still on the page, and the reading light is going pale on her hands in the daylight, and she has turned her face to the men in the vines.

body.text: She has to look past him to do it, out the window at his shoulder, and he keeps still so as not to be in the way.
He can see them past her, over her shoulder, through her window.

body: It comes at him from the side, out of nowhere, with nothing to brace for. Julian’s song: the woman in the garden who took him for the gardener, and didn’t know him until he said her name. He looks down at his hands, at the Dixie cup in them, at the knuckles, and he keeps looking at his hands until the vineyard is behind them.

journal.title: The medal
journal.text: Lena’s medal was her grandmother’s; it came back to her mother in a plastic bag. When she’s working something out, her hand goes to it. At the Point in December. Thursday at Hale’s table, about Justine. Saturday in the hall at Sully’s, about the Fishbowl. Thursday at Hale’s table, while he read out her paper about keeping quiet. Saturday in the van at dawn, on the Glory Be.

choices.text: “You said I could stop. Stop what?”
response: He says it low, under the heater, so it goes no farther than the bench. “You said I could stop. Stop what?”

She looks at the vines. The pen doesn’t move on the page. Out past the glass the men in the rows keep cutting, and the last of the frost lifts off the low ground like breath, and the question goes by with the vines, unanswered.
He doesn’t ask it twice. North of the vineyards, when it’s light enough to read by, she reaches up and turns off the reading light herself.

choices.text: *Ask her about the Saints tomorrow.*
response: “Tomorrow,” he says. “Sully’s. They letting Dale near the rope?”

It’s the one thing left they can talk about, and she steps onto it like a board she isn’t sure of, and it holds. “Dale has the rope again,” she says. “He’s rationing it. He says he’s not handing it to anybody who hasn’t bled for this team, and I said, Dale, I was *born* bleeding for this team, and he said that was my mama’s doing, not mine.” The corner of her mouth goes, and comes back. She makes a mark on the sign-up. “Are you coming?”
“I don’t know yet.”
She nods, the small nod you give a no, and goes back to her column of figures.

choices.text: *Watch the vineyards go by.*
response: He watches the vineyards. Nothing happens. The vines go by in their rows, and the men in them, and the frost, and the reading light goes on burning, pale and useless, into the daylight. He knows exactly where she is without looking, the way you know where the stove is in a dark kitchen.

s09a.slug: SATURDAY · 8:15 AM · US-101 NORTH, KING CITY → GILROY — ROW THREE
body: By King City it’s full morning, and the Salinas Valley lies open on both sides of the road, flat as a kitchen table and miles across, the fields in long brown rows waiting on spring and a few of them in winter green, irrigation pipe stacked white at the field ends, and mountains far off on either hand. The van is half awake. Joey is asleep on Tyler’s shoulder with his mouth open, and Tyler sits very straight under him, being good about it. Becca is knitting something long and red in row four, the needles going steady as a clock. Margot is writing in the notebook now that there’s light to write by, with her thermos standing between her boots. Up front Kenzie has the atlas open to a page they left an hour ago.

Out in the fields the crews are already working: a white school bus parked at the end of a row with a porta-john on a trailer hitched behind it, and a line of people in hooded sweatshirts and bandannas bent over the beds, moving down them together, setting something small and green into the dirt by hand. A tractor goes by on a dirt road with gulls behind it. Frank would have something to say about that bus, and about the union that isn’t on it, and then he’d have something to say about the price of lettuce, and both of them would be true.
Becca leans forward over the back of row three with the knitting in her lap. “Lena, what did we end up at? For Haiti?”
Lena tells her, to the cent, from memory, and Becca says, “Glory Be,” and sits back and knits faster.
Margot leans forward beside her with the notebook open. “Clarification,” she says. “The rosary before sunrise. Is that doctrine, or is that Peter?”
“That’s Peter,” Lena says, her pen still going. “Doctrine’s Peter too, if you go back far enough.”
Margot writes that down. Up front Peter, who has heard his name twice, says, “What?” and Kenzie pats his arm.

Jack keeps his face on the fields. It’s a good one. In the fall it would have been said sideways, for him, out of the corner of her mouth with one eyebrow up, and he would have been the one who laughed, and she’d have looked pleased with herself for a mile. Nobody laughs. Becca knits.

Kevin turns around in row two, carefully, so as not to wake Clare, who is asleep against the window with her mouth a little open and the rosary still in her fingers, and hooks his chin over the seat back. He keeps his voice under the engine. “Four brothers,” he says. “Javi, Luis, Nico, Tito. Oldest to youngest. I made a card.” He shows it to Jack: an index card, four names, a 49ers logo drawn badly in one corner. “What do I do.”
“Shake hands like you mean it. Look at them. Don’t call anybody sir.”
“Why not sir? Sir is respectful.”
“Clare’s a sophomore and they’re all older. Sir is for their father.”
Kevin turns back around and sits facing the windshield. Jack hears him say it to himself, under the engine, twice: “Not sir. Not sir.”

South of Soledad there’s a sign at the side of the freeway. CORRECTIONAL TRAINING FACILITY. And then, out past the fields, there it is, spread over the valley floor like a community college, except for the towers: long low buildings the color of the dirt they’re built on, fences in rows, and the lights along the fences still on in the daylight.

Rudy did six years in there. He told Jack once at the flat-top, scraping, between a short stack and a patty melt. Danny is in Trumbull, on the other side of the country, in a place that could have been built off the same drawings for all Jack knows. He knows the visiting room. The bolted tables, the vending machines along one wall, the floor wax, the guard with the newspaper; his brother’s hands around a can of Coke, because you’re allowed to buy them one. He stops there, where he always stops.
He thinks about the two lines on the flap he never read, sealed with a thumb under the heat lamp, somewhere east of here by now in a canvas sack, on their way to Leavittsburg.

He watches the place until it’s behind them. When he turns back from it, Lena is looking at him. Not at the sign. At him. She knows about Danny. In the fall she told Jack you can love somebody, but you can’t pay for them, and later she said hi to Danny himself on a collect call and told him she was going to be defense. In all of Marisol there are only a few people who would know why a man from Youngstown looks at that sign that long, and she’s one of them.

She doesn’t say anything. She takes the green thermos out from between her boots and unscrews the cap and turns it in her fingers until the chip is on her side, and fills it, and holds it out to him with the good side of the rim toward his mouth.

He takes it. He drinks from the side she gave him, slowly, so it will last to Gonzales. She goes back to the sign-up. The fences go by, and then it’s fields again, and the Soledad exit, and that’s that, as far as anybody else in the van could tell.

North of Salinas Peter starts announcing Gilroy. “Gilroy in twenty,” he tells the van. “Coffee and restrooms at Gilroy.” Then, “Gilroy in ten, people.” He has been telling Kenzie about the Starbucks at the Gilroy exit — it has a lot big enough for the van, and a drive-through, and a girl at the register who remembered him from last year — since Chualar. The outlets come up off the freeway, acres of them, and the sign for the exit, and Peter sails past it at sixty-five with his blinker off, still describing the girl at the register.
“Peter,” says Lena, and Jack says it with her, at the same instant, in the same voice, down to the note.
“I *know*,” Peter says. “I know. There’s a Denny’s in Morgan Hill.” Kenzie shuts the atlas.
“Denny’s,” says Joey, awake, from the back row, with feeling.
“We are not stopping at a Denny’s on the way to the Walk for Life,” says Bridget.
“Why not?” says Tyler.
“Because it’s a *Denny’s*, Tyler.”
“We’ll pray about it,” Peter says, and changes lanes.
Lena leans forward and sets a folded note on the dash beside the laminated route. “The garage on Washington Street,” she says. “Level two.”
“Level two, baby,” Kenzie tells Peter. “Not three. Remember three.”
“We don’t talk about three,” says Peter.

In row three they don’t look at each other. He keeps his eyes on Peter’s laminated route, three rows off, and she keeps hers on the clipboard, and the corner of her mouth has gone, and so has his. It’s the closest they’ve come to laughing together since the porch in December. He can feel it get up into his face. Beside him she puts her pen down on the column of figures and presses it there until it’s gone, and after a while his goes too.

A few miles on, with the Denny’s argument settled in the front seat and the hills closing in green on both sides, she takes her hair down, all of it, and shakes it out, and twists it back up off her neck and pushes a pencil from her bag through the knot to hold it, and picks her pen up again. She says it straight and quiet, to the window.
“Are you happy?”

He looks at the side of her face. Six hours of *Tell me if it does*, of the far end of the bench and the rim of the cup, and now this, to the window, as if the answer were hers to collect. It goes up the back of his neck, hot, before he can stop it. It’s a straight question anyway. And as it happens, for the first time in a long time, he has a straight answer.

choices.text: “Yeah. I am.”
choices.key: In the van Lena asked if you were happy. You told her the truth: yes.
response: “Yeah,” he says. “I am.”
“Good.” She caps her pen. She clips it to the board, and holds the board on her knees with both hands, and looks ahead through the windshield past Peter’s shoulder at the road.

At San Jose the van wakes up all at once — Joey first, at full volume, then the back rows, then Clare, blinking, with the rosary still in her fingers. Kenzie turns around in the front seat on her knees and starts “Holy God, We Praise Thy Name,” high and clean, and half the van comes in on the second line. Ahead the first hills of the city come up out of the haze, green, with houses stacked on them, and the valley runs out under the wheels.

choices.text: *Nod. Give her that much and no more.*
choices.key: In the van Lena asked if you were happy. You said yes.
response: He nods. “Yes.”
She nods. “Good.” The clipboard goes into her bag, and the bag goes down at her feet, and she folds her hands in her lap on top of the peacoat.

Joey wakes up at San Jose and announces it. Up front Kenzie starts a hymn, “Holy God, We Praise Thy Name,” and Becca comes in behind her strong enough for two, and then the rest of the van, and Jack, on the second verse, because he knows it, because everybody from St. Brigid’s knows it. The road climbs out of the valley into the first hills, and Peter, for the length of the hymn, doesn’t miss anything.

choices.text: “I am. Are you?”
choices.key: In the van Lena asked if you were happy. You said yes, and asked her back. She didn’t answer.
response: “I am,” he says. “Are you?”
She turns a page on the clipboard that doesn’t need turning. “Good,” she says, to his first answer, and lets the second one sit unanswered on the vinyl.

Kevin turns all the way around in row two at San Jose to tell row three that there will be water at the rally and that nobody should rely on it. Kenzie, up front, starts “Holy God, We Praise Thy Name,” and the waking van comes in a line behind her, ragged, and then together. Jack sings it. The hills come up green and close and full of houses, and the road goes up into them, and there’s no more valley to drive down.

choices.text: “Ask me after Peter finds the city.”
choices.key: In the van Lena asked if you were happy. You made a joke, and then said yes.
response: “Ask me after Peter finds the city.”
The laugh comes up in her before she can do anything about it, and she stops it with her teeth, and looks hard out the window at a field until it goes.
He gives it up. “Yeah. I am.”
“Good.”

At San Jose Peter finds the city, or a green sign with its name on it, and reads it out to the van with some dignity, and Kenzie starts “Holy God, We Praise Thy Name” to wake everybody up, and it works. The van sings its way up out of the valley into the first green hills, and the road leaves the flat behind for good.

s10.slug: SATURDAY · 11:25 AM · JUSTIN HERMAN PLAZA, THE EMBARCADERO — THE RALLY
body: Peter finds a garage off Washington Street on the second try, and by the time the fourteen of them have walked back up to the plaza the crowd runs from the foot of the Ferry Building clock to the far side of the fountain and up the steps of the hotel. Thirty-five thousand, they’re saying. Gulls work the edges for dropped bagels. The wind comes straight off the Bay, wet and smelling of the ferries’ diesel, and finds every gap in the Carhartt.

It isn’t the crowd he had in his head. It’s young — college sweatshirts from schools he’s heard of and schools he hasn’t, a high school in matching green scarves, a little girl asleep on her father’s shoulders with her sign upside down in her fist, a row of nuns in gray habits and running shoes — and there are more women in it than anybody in the van expected. Margot has her notebook open against the wind. She writes that down.

The speakers are on a stage too far off to see. What reaches the back of the plaza is the loudspeakers, every sentence arriving twice, once from the stage and once off the face of the Hyatt: a young woman who runs some kind of organization, fast and sure of herself; then a woman from Texas who ran an abortion clinic until the fall and walked out of it. The crowd goes quiet for her in a way it hasn’t for anyone else, and then very loud. Jack gets what she says in pieces. He gets the applause whole. Somewhere behind the stage a choir is singing in Latin, a little behind itself.

Skye comes across the plaza while the woman from Texas is still talking, threading through the signs with a cardboard tray of two coffees held up over her head. Black beanie, sunglasses, jeans, and his flannel, buttoned to the throat, the cuffs turned back twice so her hands can get out. He looks over at the Newman banner once, as she gets to him, and Lena’s eyes are on the flannel. They go away, down to her clipboard. He looks away too.

“I left at six,” Skye says, and puts a coffee in his hand. “I stopped in Gilroy, because I’d heard of it, and the coffee was garlic. Everything in Gilroy is garlic. I think they pump it in. These are from a cart.” She turns in a slow circle, taking it in: the signs, the nuns, the sleeping girl, the gulls. “It’s like a Lakers parade where everyone’s sad.”
“It’s a funeral that’s hopeful.”
She looks at him over the sunglasses. “That’s better than mine,” she says. “I hate that.”
On the loudspeakers the woman from Texas is talking about the day she quit. Skye tips her head at the stage. “Who’s that?”
“She ran the clinic down there. Until October.”

“And now she’s here.” Skye listens to the rest of it with the coffee forgotten under her chin, and when the plaza goes loud for the woman she doesn’t clap, and doesn’t make a joke either. She keeps listening until it’s over.

Becca gets to her first, out of the Newman knot with her scarf wound twice and her arms already open, and hugs her, coffee and all, hard enough to bring her up onto her toes. “Your letter came on St. Agnes,” Becca says into the beanie. “I’m keeping it.”
“It was mostly a surfboard,” Skye says, muffled.
“The surfboard was good.” Becca lets her go. “You got the fins right. Most people don’t.”

The Dominguez brothers come through the crowd from the Market Street side in a wedge of red caps — Javi, Luis, Nico and Tito, up from San Jose, every one of them older than Clare and built along the general lines of a door — and Kevin, who has been preparing for this since Paso Robles, says hello to all four of them in a single breath, gives his name, his major, his parish, his GPA and his position on the 49ers’ offensive line, and runs out of air.

Skye hands Jack her coffee. She steps into the middle of them and gets their names one at a time, a handshake each, saying every name back as if she’s going to be tested on it, and then she lines them up by height, out loud, in the middle of the Walk for Life. “Javi, Nico, Luis — no. Tito, stand up straight. Javi, Tito, Nico, Luis.” Tito, who hasn’t said a word yet, stands up straight. She turns to the eldest. “Javi. Joe Montana. Good Catholic? Because I have a feeling.”

Javi takes his cap off. “Notre Dame,” he says, with reverence, and after that the four of them are hers: Luis is doing the Catch with his hands, and Nico is correcting him, and Tito has begun, in a low voice, to talk.

Kevin stands beside Jack in his gloves, set free. That was supposed to be Jack’s job today — the extra man, the one who takes the brothers’ questions so Kevin doesn’t have to answer all of them at once. It’s what he came for. Kevin watches her do it in his place, and doesn’t say a word.
Margot hasn’t looked up from the notebook. Skye nods at it. “What are you studying?”
“Everyone,” says Margot, and turns the page.

Tyler and Kenzie hover at the edge of it, starstruck in the Newman way. Tyler gives her a pamphlet and a holy card of St. Gianna and tells her he’s glad she came, shining with it. Kenzie says, “I *knew* it was you at the Haiti table, I told everybody,” and holds her BlackBerry against her chest in both hands. Skye thanks Tyler and tucks the holy card into the flannel’s pocket, and asks Kenzie what she sings.
When the brothers have been handled, Lena comes over from the banner. People move for the clipboard. She stops in front of Skye and puts out her hand.
“You came,” Lena says. “You’re welcome here.”
Skye takes the hand. “I wanted to see.”
Lena nods. At the banner Peter is holding up one of the poles and calling her name, and she’s needed there.

Skye drinks her coffee. Over the lid her eyes go to the banner and come back to him — one look, not a long one — and he sees it, and she sees him see it. He hasn’t looked at the banner since. She smiles and holds her coffee under his nose, and he declines it on principle.

Two rows over, a girl in a Marquette sweatshirt lifts a phone. Skye’s smile starts — he sees it start, the bright practiced thing coming up into her face by itself, the way a knee comes up for the doctor’s hammer — and stops halfway. She pulls the beanie down to her eyebrows, turns her back on the phone and puts her face in his shoulder as if she’s cold. It isn’t her day. Jack moves half a step to the left, so that the girl in the Marquette sweatshirt gets a very good picture of the back of a Carhartt.

At ten past twelve the loudspeakers say something about the route that nobody at the back can make out, and the front of the crowd begins to move, and then the middle. The Newman banner comes up off the pavement on its two poles. Somebody behind them starts the rosary.

journal.title: Becca Lindell
journal.text: Coeur d’Alene. Seven siblings; wants seven or nine kids, odd numbers, for the tiebreaker. Can butcher a deer — elk too. Has pulled a calf, and it shows. Ran the beach cleanup like a cattle drive and put me on her team. Asked about the scar in the water. Told her mother the cleanup was a date, then asked me if it was. Wrote FRIDAY? on her clipboard, and meant it. Drives her brother Eli’s red Ranger; St. Isidore on the visor. Second date: Friday-night football. Knows downs. Prayed a Glory Be on fourth and one. Learned the First Way on the bleachers and said it back perfectly. Kissed my cheek so there’s no confusion. Third date was mine. I asked. I paid. The elephant seals at Piedras Blancas at sunset, in Kevin’s Odyssey. She knew what every one of them weighed. Nobody’s ever planned a thing for her, she says. She’s been praying for two in the morning. Named a hermit crab Thomas, after the First Way, and asked Fr. Osei whose blessing it was. Works the Marine Lab touch tank Thursday afternoons and Friday at six in the morning — that’s how she signed Thomas out. He’s home; she knows him by the chip in his shell. Mailed Rosie a birthday card with Thomas on it and six true facts on the back, to the address I gave her for her Christmas cards. She does them in October. Has a page on her clipboard for Wes. She’s been praying for him and Lena since September. Her eyes are gray. Brought a survival bag to the library for my midterm, with a clementine for Lena. Prays at two, like always. Took me to *Where the Wild Things Are* at the Rialto; her favorite line is the last one. My mother wrote her a thank-you note. Her list for Halloween says WE SHOULD MATCH!! It’s due Halloween. She says I look at her like homework. She says she’ll wait. Stuck on the touch tank all weekend while we were at Big Sur: the weekend volunteer has the swine flu. Asked me for the monks’ fruitcake for her Grandma Agnes — the only honest fruitcake in America. I handed in my homework six days early. St. Isidore and St. Maria: her first. Early, she said. Nobody’s early but her. Halloween: she sewed my costume out of a Rathdrum Feed & Seed sack. She was St. Maria de la Cabeza in Mrs. Fitch’s lace, with a water jug. Best Saint, by acclamation — a gold halo. Never won anything that wasn’t a heifer. Home at 11:40 for the six o’clock tank; the volunteer still has the flu. ‘Farmer.’ Theo’s birthday: huckleberry jam from her mother, for Theo — the Idaho gift. Next to his mother all night. ‘He’s *mine*. Since the beach cleanup.’ Toasted St. Martin de Porres: a dog and a cat and a mouse, one bowl. The Portolá steps, November 4th: her mom’s been calling me her boyfriend since September. She asked if she could tell her she’s right. I said yes. Her mom first, then Facebook. She flies home to Spokane the Wednesday before Thanksgiving. Her mother has named the turkey. She asked how I’m getting home. Greyhound. She frowned. Her mother sent a box: socks, cookies, two jars of huckleberry — JACK, and FOR THE CATHOLIC ROOMMATE. She offered me Daisy’s money. Six hundred and twelve dollars. It’s there, she says. Daisy doesn’t mind. Saturday, Ohio State in overtime: she gave me a photograph of the elephant seals in a frame she painted, every seal labeled with what it weighs. She’ll call during her dad’s grace on Thanksgiving so I can hear it. She wants to watch Michigan here, with me. ‘Someday I want to see your house. Is that okay to say?’ Ma wrote her. Three days after Christmas. Pittsburgh’s cheaper than Cleveland. She looked. Wednesday, in Eli’s truck, I told her. She said she did everything right, and she did. ‘It just isn’t the thing, is it.’ She asked me to leave it up on Facebook till she’s told her mom at the table. Thursday at two she texted. Still praying for me — not a girlfriend thing, she says. At the twelve-ten she turned around across the aisle at the sign of peace and held out her hand. Then she held it out to Lena. At the airport, a week to the day: St. Raphael, for Nonna. Father Osei read the name at the twelve-ten, and she heard. Thanksgiving: told her mom at the table. Texted me first — happy Thanksgiving, praying for Nonna, taking it down now. Then she did. The Immaculate Conception, on the steps after the 12:10: white elephant, ten dollars, nothing that eats. Thomas is going home to Idaho in a Tupperware to see snow. The Advent party: ran the white elephant like a cattle auction. Three steals and it’s frozen. Her Christmas card found me in the lobby on finals Monday — six true facts about hermit crabs; number six, they need a friend. She sent my family one too, praying for Nonna’s hand, and Ma stood it at the front of the mantel. Christmas Eve she wrote on my Wall. The first day back, on the steps of St. Brendan’s, she said she saw, and she’s happy for me. Over Christmas she prayed I’d be happy. Thomas saw snow. At the Haiti table: her grandmother prayed that rosary at the gate of the Sunshine Mine in 1972, eight days. On the eighth day two men came up. She lent Skye her apron. Skye wrote her a letter, on paper. It came on St. Agnes, with a surfboard drawn on the back. At the Walk for Life she hugged Skye and told her she’s keeping the letter.

choices.text: *Walk her in with Newman. She’s with you.*
response: He takes her hand and walks her into the Newman crowd behind the banner — in among Becca and Tyler and Joey and the brothers, in front of every phone in the plaza, his hand around hers where anybody can see it. She lets herself be walked. Her fingers are cold and they hold on.
Peter, walking backward to count heads, hands her a sign off the stack without looking at who she is. She reads it, and looks up at Jack, and hands it to Tito, who is taller.

choices.text: “She’s here for the anthropology.”
response: “She’s here for the anthropology,” Jack tells Tyler, who asked.
Margot, still writing: “That’s mine.”

“We can share,” Skye says. “You take the women. I’ll take the men.” She hooks one arm through Javi’s and the other through Jack’s and steps off with one of them on each side, and Javi walks the first block like somebody who’s been asked to a dance.

choices.text: *Let her pick where she walks. She’s better at rooms.*
response: He doesn’t place her. He lets her look, and she looks over the moving crowd once, quick, reading it — where the phones are, where the cameras on poles are, where the light is — and picks: a few yards behind the Newman banner, beside Clare and the brothers, where four sets of shoulders in red caps stand between her and most of the plaza. She puts him on her other side.
“Good spot,” he says.
“Best in the house,” says Skye, and takes his arm.
