s11.slug: SATURDAY · 12:10 PM · THE EMBARCADERO — “EXPLAIN IT WHILE WE WALK”
body: The Embarcadero opens out ahead of them, wide and flat and lined with palms, the Bay alongside it gray-blue and the piers going by in their numbered sheds, and the march fills it curb to curb and moves along it at the speed of the slowest stroller. The Newman banner is a few yards ahead: Peter on one pole and Lena on the other, two backs and a bedsheet of painted letters. Clare walks near the curb with her rosary, her lips going.
“You explain it while we walk,” Skye says. “That’s the rule.”
“We’re barely walking.”
“Then explain it slowly.” She tucks her arm through his. “Start where it starts. You always start where it starts.”

So he starts where it starts. That it’s somebody from the beginning — not a someday somebody, a somebody, small. That every line anybody has drawn after that point is somebody bigger deciding who counts, and the people who get to decide who counts have a long record, and most of it is terrible. That he didn’t get it off a pamphlet. He got it out of Aquinas and a biology textbook, in that order, and then in the other order, and they came out in the same place.

“Aquinas and a biology textbook,” Skye says. “My tutor would have wept.” She bumps him with her hip. “My turn.” She counts on the fingers of the hand that isn’t holding his arm. “Since I was twelve, my body has had a board of directors. My mother. Skylark. Wardrobe. The network. When I was fifteen, a man at the network I’d met twice sent a note about my weight, and my mother put it on the refrigerator under a magnet shaped like a strawberry, so I’d see it at breakfast. I have had my hair cut on a vote.” She is walking faster. “It is the one thing — the *one* thing — that’s mine to decide. And every girl should get to decide it. It isn’t a bumper sticker to me, Jack. It’s the only room in the building I have a key to.”

She’s walking faster with every sentence, faster than the march, nearly up on the heels of the family in front of them. He slows down. He walks at the speed of the stroller, on purpose, and because her arm is through his she has to slow down with him; after a few yards she does, and her voice comes down with her feet.

“It’s your body,” he says. “I’m not arguing about your body. I’d fight the network about your body. I’d fight your mother.” She snorts. “But the kid isn’t your body. It’s in it. It’s got its own heart going by six weeks, its own blood type. Half of it isn’t even yours. Here’s my whole argument: nobody gets to own anybody. Not a network. Not a mother. Not a man. That’s it. That’s the argument, and it’s yours too.”
He has got louder than he meant to, and a man in a Knights of Columbus jacket turns around to nod at him. Skye watches the man turn back.
“His family said he was out of his mind,” she says.
“That’s the Gospel for today.”
“I know. I read ahead. I always read ahead.” She pats his arm. “Fine. A philosopher.”

She had a tutor on set, she tells him, the year she was sixteen, because the State of California requires a minor on a soundstage to be educated between setups, and the tutor was a grad student from UCLA who was bored to death with algebra and gave her an essay by a woman at MIT instead. “You wake up in a hospital bed,” Skye says, “back to back with a famous violinist. He’s unconscious. He has a kidney thing, and you’re the only match, so the Society of Music Lovers kidnapped you in the night and plugged him into you. Nine months and he’s cured. Unplug, and he dies. Do you have to stay?” She lets a woman with a double stroller go by. “I read that in a trailer, in a school uniform from wardrobe, with a crew of sixty outside waiting for me to finish my homework so they could get paid. The famous one, kept alive on somebody else’s body. Believe me, I noticed. And I still think she’s right. You don’t have to stay plugged in. Nobody gets to make you.”

“The violinist’s a stranger,” Jack says. “You got kidnapped for him. It’s a great argument about strangers.” He looks up the road at the bedsheet letters and back at her. “A kid’s the one person on earth you didn’t have to be kidnapped to owe anything to. Your mother didn’t have to be kidnapped to owe you something. She owed you because she’s your —”
He hears it on the way out. It’s too late to get it back.

Skye looks at him. “Careful,” she says, mildly. And then she plays the harder card off the top of her own deck. “The woman who wrote it built it for the worst case, you know. The kidnapping is the worst case. She says so.”

“I know.” He walks a few steps. “That’s the one I don’t have a speech for. I have the same answer, and I know what it costs somebody who isn’t me to hear it. I’m not going to pretend I know what it costs.”

She studies him, walking, and doesn’t push it; what she wanted, apparently, was to see whether he’d make a speech. “I’ve known girls who did it,” she says. “On sets. Sixteen. Nineteen. One of them was better than I’ll ever be. She drove herself, on a Friday, and on Monday she hit every mark and every line, and she wasn’t a monster, Jack. Some of them were sad about it. Some of them were glad.”

“I don’t think she’s a monster.” He means to stop there and doesn’t. “Dorothy Day had an abortion. Nineteen-nineteen; she was twenty-one. She wrote about it, and she grieved it as long as she lived, and she spent the rest of her life feeding people. If she’s a monster, I don’t know what the rest of us are.”
Skye looks at him sideways. “That’s your best one,” she says. “You saved it.”

They are passing a group of women walking together near the curb, older, forties and fifties, in parkas and sneakers, carrying signs that say what they did, and that they regret it. Some are hand-lettered and some are printed; there’s a year on one, a first name on another. Skye has walked past ten thousand slogans since the plaza without slowing down. She slows down here. She reads the nearest sign to the bottom, her lips moving a little, and the woman carrying it — gray-blond, in a Giants scarf — nods to her, and Skye nods back, and for a while she doesn’t argue anything at all.
“They’re not saying it to me,” she says finally, low. “That’s what gets me. They’re not trying to win anything. They’re just — carrying it.”
A few yards off, walking with Clare’s brothers, Margot has stopped writing. She has the cap of her pen against her lip and her eyes on Skye, and she is listening.

When Skye starts again it’s quieter, and it’s the best thing she’s said all day. “Here’s what I’d tell this crowd if they gave me the stage. This is cheap. Thirty-five thousand people and a choir is cheap, if nobody pays for the girl at nineteen in a town like yours. Who pays her rent? Who drives her to the appointment, when the boyfriend’s gone to Akron and her mother won’t look at her across the table? The woman on the stage?” She stops walking, and a family with a wagon steers around them. “You?”

choices.text: “That’s your argument — nobody gets to own anybody. I’m just extending it.”
choices.key: On the Walk for Life you told Skye you were only extending her own argument. She made you answer who pays the girl’s rent, and walked the whole way.
response: “That’s your argument,” Jack says. “That nobody gets to own anybody. I’m just extending it. To the kid.”
“That’s a good line,” Skye says, “and it’s a line.” She starts walking again. “I asked you who pays her rent.”

And she makes him answer it — not the kid, the girl — for the length of the next pier, and the one after it, and the one after that. He does it badly. He has the parishes back home that pay a girl’s rent and don’t ask her name; he has the women from a pregnancy center who drive mothers to every appointment in their own cars; he has to admit there aren’t enough of either. She takes that one. She takes it in front of a Knight of Columbus who has been listening since the plaza, and the Knight nods at her.

choices.text: “You’re right that it’s cheap if nobody pays for the girl after.”
choices.key: On the Walk for Life you told Skye she was right: it’s cheap if nobody pays for the girl after. She walked the whole way.
response: “You’re right,” Jack says. “It’s cheap if nobody pays for the girl after.”
She stands in the middle of the Embarcadero with her mouth open, and the march goes around them on both sides like water around a piling.
“Say it at the next pier,” she says.

He says it at the next pier. He adds what he has: the parishes back home that pay a girl’s rent and don’t ask her name, the women from a pregnancy center who drive mothers to every appointment in their own cars — and that there aren’t enough of them, nowhere near. She wins the girl at nineteen, outright, and he gives it to her. He keeps the kid. She lets him keep it, for now. She has the trophy.

choices.text: “The girl at nineteen and the kid — I don’t think you get to pick one.”
choices.key: On the Walk for Life you told Skye it’s the girl and the kid both, or you’re lying. She walked the whole way.
response: “The girl at nineteen and the kid,” Jack says. “I don’t think you get to pick one. I think it’s both or you’re lying.”
“Then you’re going to lose a lot of arguments,” Skye says. “In this crowd too.”
“I know.”
She looks past him at the women with the signs, and then at the march going by, the sweatshirts and the nuns and the Knights, and back at him. “How many?”

He thinks about it honestly. He loses it at Newman about once a week — to Margot, to the guy who says the march is the work. He loses it at his own kitchen table. He walks anyway. He tells her so, and she wins that one: she makes him say, on the Embarcadero, that his own side doesn’t do both either, and she counts it.

choices.text: “You’ve been incorporated since twelve. The kid hasn’t even been incorporated.”
choices.key: On the Walk for Life you told Skye the kid hasn’t even been incorporated. She made you pay for it, and walked the whole way.
response: “You’ve been incorporated since twelve,” Jack says. “The kid hasn’t even been incorporated.”
Skye stops dead in the middle of the Walk for Life. “Oh, that’s *good*,” she says, loud enough that the Knight of Columbus turns around again. “That’s very good. You’re going to pay for it.”

And she makes him. She makes him pay for the next half mile — the long stretch past the piers, with tourists at the rails looking down at them — and she wins it. A corporation, she points out, at least gets a lawyer. A corporation has an accountant in Encino and a board and a mother who signs for it, and the girl at nineteen has a Greyhound schedule and a boyfriend who stopped answering, and if he’s going to make jokes about personhood he’d better be ready to hire her one. He isn’t. He says so. She takes the half mile.

s11a.slug: SATURDAY · 1:20 PM · THE EMBARCADERO, THE SIDEWALK — A MAN WITH A MEGAPHONE
body: Past the piers the sidewalk on the left belongs to the other side: a few dozen people, with a couple of bicycle cops leaning on their handlebars at the end of the block, and hand-lettered signs and a megaphone and a chant that rhymes rosaries with ovaries and has advice for the marchers about where to keep each.

The man with the megaphone is in his sixties — a gray ponytail, a fleece vest, a sign under his arm lettered on the back of a calendar page with a woman’s name and a year, DENISE · 1969, and nothing else. The year is from before Roe. He has been working the march for blocks, and the march has been letting him.

Then he sees Clare. She’s at the edge of the crowd by the curb with her rosary wound through her fingers, her lips moving, her eyes down, and he comes off the sidewalk at her with the megaphone a foot from her face and says things into it that are crude and close and built to hurt a nineteen-year-old girl, and the megaphone makes every one of them enormous.
Clare keeps praying. The beads go through her fingers at the same speed.
Skye lets go of Jack’s arm and steps in between them.
“She’s nineteen and she’s praying,” Skye says. “Yell at me. I’m on your side.”

The man stops. He looks at her — the beanie, the sunglasses, a man’s flannel buttoned to the throat — and he has no idea who she is; it isn’t anywhere in his face. After a moment he gets it, or gets a version of it, and he turns the megaphone on her. “Then what are you *doing* in there?” His voice cracks on the top of it. “You’re worse than they are. They don’t know any better. You know better and you walk with them anyway.”
The heat comes up the back of Jack’s neck and into his face, fast — it only comes like that now when somebody goes at her — and his hand closes on the cup.
Without looking around, Skye puts one hand back against his chest, and she leaves it there.
“Sir,” she says to the man, pleasantly, at the volume of a dinner party. “I’m agreeing with you. Agree back quieter.”

The sidewalk laughs — his own side, a woman with a wire coat hanger on her sign, a kid in a beret — and a few people on the march laugh with them. The man’s face goes dark red. He brings the megaphone back up.

Ahead at the banner Lena has turned around at the noise, the pole in both hands, and she is looking at Skye. A few yards behind them Kenzie has her BlackBerry up, and has had it up since the man came off the sidewalk.
And Jack is still lit, under Skye’s hand, with the megaphone coming back up a foot from her face.

journal.title: Clare Dominguez
journal.text: Clare Dominguez. Newman sophomore. Plays violin in the Mass band. Played ‘Ashokan Farewell’ at the Haiti table and people stopped on the lawn. Kevin’s mother knows her mother. Everybody’s mother knows her mother. Four brothers, back in San Jose. Knows football better than Kevin. Wore a 49ers cap to Sully’s. At the Walk for Life a man with a megaphone screamed at her, and she kept praying. Skye stood in front of her.

choices.text: *Step up to him.*
response: He steps up. He gets one step, and her hand stops him — closes on his shirt through the open jacket and holds, with more in it than he’d have guessed was in her arm.
“Down, Ohio,” she says, without turning around.

The man looks at Jack, all six feet of him, and at the girl holding him back by a fistful of shirt, and finishes what he had to say a good deal faster than he meant to, and returns to the curb with his calendar page.
A block on, her arm back through his and her eyes on the road, Skye says, “You were going to loom at a man at the Walk for Life.”
“I wasn’t going to do anything.”
“You were going to loom. Professionally. I felt it through the shirt.” She walks a few steps. “I’m not going to say anything about it now. I’m saving it for later. I have plans for it.”

choices.text: *Let her handle it. Stand where he can see you.*
response: He doesn’t step up. He stays exactly where he is, at her shoulder, close enough that she can feel him there, and lets the man look at him.

The man looks — up, at a kid from Youngstown in a work jacket who isn’t saying a word — and the rest of what he has comes out faster, and shorter, and more to the sidewalk than to her. The megaphone comes down. He turns away with the calendar page under his arm.

Skye keeps her hand where it is until the man is back on the curb. Only then does she take Jack’s arm again, and they walk on, and she doesn’t say anything for a block, and then she says, very fast, “You’re a very good wall. Ten out of ten.”

choices.text: *Hand the man a coffee.*
response: He holds out the coffee. It’s the one she carried across the plaza for him, two-thirds gone and stone cold.
“It’s cold,” Jack says, “but it isn’t from Gilroy. You sound like you could use it.”

The sidewalk laughs again, harder, both sides of it. And the man, astonishingly — after he has looked at the cup, and at Jack, and at the girl with her hand on Jack’s chest — takes it. He doesn’t drink it. He carries it back to the sidewalk in one hand with the megaphone in the other, and stands there holding both. “He’s going to drink it,” Skye says into Jack’s sleeve, walking. “I’ve lost an argument to a coffee.”

s12.slug: SATURDAY · 2:25 PM · THE END OF THE ROUTE — THE VAN AT THE CURB
body: At the end of the route the Walk comes apart into what it was made of. Church groups stand in knots on the sidewalk counting heads. Buses with the names of parishes taped inside their windshields wait three deep at the curb with their engines running, and a man in a Knights of Columbus jacket is folding a banner the length of a living room by himself, corner to corner, very carefully, on the pavement. The sun is low and white on the Bay, and everybody on the curb is squinting.

Peter has brought the van around from the garage on Washington Street and has it at the curb with its hazards going and its back doors open, and the Newman people are feeding signs into it in stacks. Kevin is down the block saying goodbye to the Dominguez brothers, one long handshake at a time. Skye left a few minutes ago in a cab, to get the Saab out of a garage at the other end of the route. Margot sits on the back bumper with her thermos between her boots, the only one not loading anything.

Lena is at the side door with the clipboard, counting the van back in, the pencil through the knot of her hair. She does it by face, as she did at five this morning in the dark, and when she gets to him she makes the tick without lifting her eyes. “Short two,” she tells the clipboard. Peter comes down the curb on his circuit, and she says, “Joey’s at the Ferry Building, in the restroom. Becca went to get him,” and Peter says, “Ten past,” and goes on to tell the buses.
For the first time since five this morning neither of them has anything to carry.
“*Look*,” Kenzie is saying at the back doors, holding her BlackBerry out to Bridget in both hands. “It’s already got twenty-two.” Jack sees it over their shoulders.

body: His own name is in the gray line at the bottom. Kenzie sees him reading and beams up at him. “I tagged you! I couldn’t tag her. We’re not friends.” Then Bridget wants to see the one of Clare again, and the two of them carry the phone and an armful of signs around to the far side of the van.
Lena has seen it. Kenzie has been showing it to the curb for ten minutes. She writes something in the margin of the clipboard and says, at an ordinary volume, “It’s a prayer.”
He looks at her.

“Thirty-five thousand people walked two miles today for children nobody got to name, and for their mothers.” The pencil goes down the list. “It is not a premiere. And now it’s Cassidy from Sweetwater on Kenzie’s wall, and half of Newman will have liked it before Peter finds the freeway.”
The pencil stops at the bottom of the column. “Some people are very good at keeping quiet,” she says. “You said so.”

“She didn’t post anything.” He can hear his voice coming up and keeps it where it is. “She wouldn’t. A girl put a phone up at her at the rally and she turned around and gave it the back of her head. I watched her do it. Kenzie posted that.” His hand goes out toward the far side of the van, where Kenzie is. “She drove up here alone at six in the morning to see a thing she doesn’t believe in. She walked two miles of it arguing with me, and she listened — she read those women’s signs, every one, she slowed down for them. And when that guy came off the sidewalk at Clare with a megaphone, she’s the one who stood in front of her.” He looks at the banner pole, leaning against the van’s side with the Newman banner rolled around it. “Which one of us did that?”
It’s a shot, and it goes in. She was at the banner, turned around with the pole in both hands, a few yards up the road. She isn’t a coward; he knows that better than anybody. It goes in anyway.
When she looks up from the clipboard, it’s straight at him.
“You brought your girlfriend to the Walk for Life, Jack.”

He has a list, and the back hall at Sully’s is at the top of it, where she called Skye a performance and wouldn’t say what she meant. He doesn’t understand that one any better than the rest. Not understanding her used to make him careful with her. He can feel what it makes him now — in his jaw, in the hands in his pockets. He says none of it. All of it goes into what he does say.

choices.text: *Say it low, so she has to hear every word.*
choices.key: At the end of the Walk you asked Lena, low, how she had the nerve to be mad at you. She didn’t answer. She left.
response: He steps in close — close enough that the people at the back doors can’t hear him over the buses, close enough that she has nowhere to look but at him, close enough to see the pencil through her hair and the bitten place on it near the lead. He keeps it low, so she has to stand there and take every word.
“How do you have the nerve to be mad at me? For any of this?”

choices.text: *Say it loud enough for the curb.*
choices.key: At the end of the Walk you asked Lena, loud enough for the whole curb, how she had the nerve to be mad at you. She didn’t answer. She left.
response: It comes up out of him at the volume of the megaphone an hour ago. In the back of the van a sign slides off the top of the stack and slaps flat on the asphalt, and lies there.
“How do you have the nerve to be mad at me? For any of this?”

choices.text: *Say it like a fact. Don’t raise your voice.*
choices.key: At the end of the Walk you asked Lena, like a fact, how she had the nerve to be mad at you. She didn’t answer. She left.
response: He keeps his hands in the pockets of the Carhartt. He doesn’t raise his voice, and he doesn’t lower it. He says it level, no louder than the buses, a number off a scoreboard. It has been sitting in him for weeks.
“How do you have the nerve to be mad at me? For any of this?”

choices.text: *Start with a joke and watch it turn.*
choices.key: At the end of the Walk you started with a joke and asked Lena how she had the nerve to be mad at you. She didn’t answer. She left.
response: “You know Peter missed Gilroy,” he says. “And the garage. Twice. He took fourteen people around the same three blocks of Washington Street till Joey started praying for him by name, and out of all fourteen of us, somehow I’m the one who doesn’t know where he’s —” Halfway through it, the joke dies in his mouth, and what was under it all along comes up instead.
“How do you have the nerve to be mad at me? For any of this?”

body.text: Every head at the back of the van has turned. Bridget is holding a sign in both hands in front of her like a shield, and on the bumper Margot has stopped with the thermos cup halfway to her mouth.
Behind the van the sign-loading goes on, a stack at a time, every back to them. On the bumper Margot has the thermos cup at her mouth and isn’t drinking from it.

body: Lena doesn’t say anything. She has the clipboard flat against her chest with both arms crossed over it, and her mouth opens on something — he sees it come, right there, whatever it is — and closes on it. Her eyes stay on his face. A bus with ST. ANNE’S taped in its windshield pulls out from the curb behind her, and the wind off it moves her hair, and she doesn’t blink.
And then it turns. Her knuckles go white on the edge of the clipboard, one hand and then the other. Whatever she had in her mouth goes back down, and her chin comes up.
“Thank you for coming, Jack,” she says.
She tucks the clipboard under her arm. He doesn’t see which way she goes. He’s looking at his hands, which have nothing in them and have started, at the ends of the fingers, to shake.
Peter comes back down the curb and says, “Ten past,” to Jack, and then gets a look at his face and says it again, more gently, and doesn’t stop to find out why.
At the back of the van Margot screws the cup onto the thermos, a full turn at a time, and stands up off the bumper, and starts handing signs up into the van with the rest of them.

journal.title: Lena Broussard
journal.text: New Orleans. Two seventeen. Classics. Hale paired us for the semester. Makes a roux like she’s taking a vow and expects you to keep up. Her father sells Gulf shrimp — Broussard’s Seafood, Banks Street. Boyfriend: Wes Arceneaux — Tulane, civil engineering, the boat at sixteen. Calls at 8:04 on the dot. Her grandmother, Lucille Guidry, died in the storm in ’05; they buried her in November, in the good dress. The medal came back to her mother in a plastic bag. She has never asked her mother one question. The year after, she went to Mass every morning to yell at God, and somewhere in there it stopped being a fight. Paints a mean fleur-de-lis. Said hi to Danny. Says she’s going to be defense. Walked her home the long way from Pi Lam: the beach, the creek, the tower, the Commons, the Lagoon bench. Wes calls from somewhere loud lately; her brother Luc is with him. She’s decided not to notice. The Tuesday of the wake he called on the dot, from his room. He came for Columbus Day weekend to see the Pacific. She’d told him it’s a threat. He touched it at two in the morning. Came to Marisol for the money, she says — Notre Dame gave her half. Went to Hale’s office to tell him he was wrong about who gets to forgive. Cried for Anders on the roof and didn’t give an inch. Stayed till the chimes. There’s a sentence she hasn’t finished. Her middle name is Thérèse; October first is her feast. She erased *Show Lena* out of the Hopkins herself, so Danny could have it. At midnight I gave her *Story of a Soul* with my margins in it, and she wouldn’t let me erase a word. On the beach she asked if I know what I’m doing. I don’t. She laughed. At the elevator: ‘That was a terrible thing to be glad about.’ Brought Wes to everything. Wouldn’t walk past the last house on Seacliff toward the Point; said she was cold. At the stove she gave Becca the spoon. Monday night, two floors down, on the phone to New Orleans: ‘He’s my friend, Wes.’ Plays the piano in the Delgado basement — the one nobody admits to playing. Two years at the Rosary. At five in the morning she played the Saints on the Ferrer carillon with her fists, one bell flat, and said it wasn’t flat, it was New Orleans. Wes told her what I said on the beach, and what I didn’t. On a motel porch above Lucia at three in the morning she told me I can’t say her name like that. She asked what I decided. Not to be the one who wrecks anything, I said. She said okay. Then: me neither. Bought her Mémère a fruitcake from the monks, in exact change. ‘A girl writes the thing she wants first, Youngstown.’ Halloween: Flannery O’Connor, with a stuffed peacock tagged 57. Andalusia. She wouldn’t go past the last house on Seacliff, not even for Laney. ‘I came as her. I never said she was right.’ In the last minute of the extra hour, she put my hat back on. All Souls: she wrote her grandmother’s name in the book, and Nora Calloway’s. Nora was her host at Preview Weekend, in April. That night Wes ended it, on the phone, on the east stairs. He stopped going to Mass in September. There’s a ring. She knew something in September and decided not to notice — she says she’s good at it. At six in the morning she asked me what I’m going to do. She wrote Hale twelve pages in the spring of ’08, two years after the year she yelled at God. She’s had the same postcard the whole time. She knew mine on the porch. She had a house picked out on Zimple Street. A fig tree. She’d picked the paint. Veterans Day, on the bench above Campus Point: St. Martin gave the beggar half his cloak; she says everybody forgets the beggar took it. No. 9 for the reliquary. Friday the 13th, under the eucalyptus, in the middle of a sentence about monarchs: Julian asked her to dinner. So. Thursday night in the basement she played the piano properly — around the dead F. The last time she played it right in front of anybody was a November, four years ago. If you play well, she says, people ask you to play. Reading *New Moon* out of spite. Friday she signed the Manhattan Declaration from bed, with a cold. Two soups. She ate Julian’s. Mine’s on the sill for tomorrow. Ate Gloria’s soup cold out of the quart, at the sill, at six in the morning. Argued YES: a promise is made to a person, not to a reason. Wrote on my paper that I don’t believe one sentence of it. Neither does she. Mémère is lighting a candle for Nonna — the whole name. Half a name is half a candle. At the airport: Our Lady of Prompt Succor, for Nonna. She works fast. Thanksgiving: Theo said *pop* to the whole Broussard table. She asked about Theo, and Nonna, and her saint. Julian called during grace. Wes was in the kitchen. ‘Go back to your family, Youngstown.’ Handed Julian the bell rope at Sully’s. Knows I don’t work Mondays. Texted at two in the morning about Yusuf’s mother. On the lawn at four, looking at the place I wasn’t. Came to the Anchor at the end of my shift in Kevin’s car — Julian’s in Oakland, his brother’s home from the Navy. She has a paper. St. Nicholas Eve: Walgreens at half past one. I told her about Ma’s two hundred shoes; she said then we’re doing it, and we did every door in Delgado. Says I hold my phone like a hand of cards. Asked where I go. I said sometime. She said okay. Book Nine, for her Greek final: *Outis*. Nobody. In the laundry room she stepped back first. ‘Don’t make me be the one who wrecks something.’ Julian’s writing something she can’t hear yet. Twelve and oh in overtime. Her free hand found Kevin. Knows Book Nine by heart; asked me to pray at eight. Picked my best argument at the Brick: what a man says yes to. Put her phone face up next to mine and said nothing. Heard Julian’s song before anybody. ‘It’s good, Jack. It’s really good.’ Told me not to leave in the second chorus. The Advent party: I kept the whole room between us all night. She brought coffee to the white elephant, and I got it. Stole my 8-Ball. Won an argument about ‘Joy to the World’ with Isaac Watts. Didn’t play. Julian did. Friday night, half past twelve, she knocked on 412; Theo said the library. At the Mañanitas she told me about Juan Diego, who took the long way around the hill. Thirteen and oh. She texted me the number. After the Gaudete Mass she asked the 8-Ball something. Better not tell you now. Geminids from the roof without me. At Hale’s oral she’d answered him in Augustine — said my sentence was his. She defended it and won, and told him to ask where I say yes at two in the morning. Julian kissed her goodbye at his car; he’s going to New Orleans for New Year’s. Friday she knocked with two coffees and a list of every place. She played the basement piano for me, properly. Taught me a secret in the O Antiphons. Pecan at Gloria’s counter; fourteen and oh is ordained. On the Lighthouse porch she said it plain: I’d never not answered her before. Never missed Sully’s. Always came to her, whatever it was — and now I stay away. She knows something’s hurting. She didn’t make me say what. Walked past the last house to the Point for the first time all semester. The bonfires on the levee on Christmas Eve — call her from the garage. On the roof I nearly said it. The 8-Ball said ask again later. She gave me the tin to keep. I gave her Benedict. At the checkpoint she turned around and said something I couldn’t hear. Christmas week: her sister had the baby in the third quarter of the Dallas game, while they were still undefeated, so Beau didn’t get a vote. Lucille Odile — both grandmothers. Lena’s the godmother. Then they lost. The 8-Ball said very doubtful. She texts me the O Antiphons at dusk. Monday night she called at ten to one to argue about Pius, and won the point fair. I told her I’ve been sleeping in Danny’s bed. She said somebody ought to. When the Pope went down she texted within the minute: is he alright, are you. Christmas Eve she held the phone up to a bonfire on the levee so I could hear it burn. After Midnight Mass she wrote from the steps of Holy Rosary: an hour behind me, like she said. She’d mailed me *The Moviegoer* before the last night. Christmas night she told me how Réveillon went, and about the place her mother sets for her grandmother. Then she said her mama worked at Memorial. Nothing else. Holy Family: they lost to Tampa in overtime — ‘They’re resting.’ Fr. Dom took the short form; hers read the long one, and we’re not discussing it. Sunday night we whispered for two hours because Nonna was asleep in her chair, and she whispered too, from her back steps. I read her her own margins; she argued with the girl who wrote them. I told her Dad went in. ‘And Danny drank it.’ Julian calls at ten his time. Tuesday she called from behind the register at her father’s market — home field; her father’s making the musician a gumbo. I told her what Danny asked about the third. If Pop won’t get out of the truck, she says, I get in. She said she wouldn’t call as much. Then she said she’d call. Wednesday nothing. Thursday at dawn, the morning after Julian landed, she called from the river with beignets. She said she’d call. She asked if I asked Ma who the candle was for. No. You don’t. New Year’s Eve she texted at my midnight, an hour early for her. At hers it came the second the year turned — before the fireworks. I know what that means. Then the river on fire, and Julian beside it. New Year’s Day I called her from the garage at the half, and she said, You called *me*. Saturday night she called the house — Ma answered and talked to her for ten minutes. Two hours on the kitchen phone, her mother’s cordless dying twice. Her grandmother made the christening gown for Luc in 1985; it rode out the storm in Mémère’s cedar chest in Breaux Bridge. She had me be the priest so she could practice the promises. She thinks Binx doesn’t stop looking — he stops looking by himself. I told her Danny asked me something I can’t answer yet; she didn’t ask what. She asked how California was. ‘Come back, Youngstown.’ Two hours, and she never said Julian’s name. Lucille was baptized in the third quarter, and she didn’t get one word wrong. After that I called every night. Twelfth Night she got the baby in the king cake. Friday she said she hasn’t been fair to Julian, and she’s going to fix it. Sunday she landed: come find me tomorrow. Monday I couldn’t find her — not at 217, not at the twelve-ten. She came into Hale’s seminar a step behind him with a king cake, and the only chair left was next to mine. She was polite to me for fifteen minutes. Then Dido. Tuesday morning Julian put up a picture from their dinner Monday — birthday dinner, two days late. She’s tagged. She’d said call me after. I didn’t. At the mailboxes she asked about my break, and I told her as far as Denver, and Ma’s words about the coffee. ‘Tell her I’m glad.’ The baptism was lovely. Tuesday night at St. Brendan’s she had the whole thing organized by half past eight, in a whisper, and put me on the table with Becca. When the TV said trapped she left the room. Julian went. Wednesday at the table she met Skye. She said no pictures at the table, and I argued with her about it in front of everybody. That night at the desk: Skye’s envelope was the biggest. ‘Tell her thank you. From Newman.’ Thursday she took the far end of Hale’s table before anybody got there. She moved the Saints to Sully’s. Saturday in the back hall she said she changed her mind, and stood up for Laney, and said Skye gave a good performance, and wouldn’t say what she meant. At Atlanta she kept my chair till the half. At ten after three she told me the time. Wednesday at three in the morning, the aftershock, in the Fishbowl: she said I could stop whatever I’m doing. I don’t know what I’m doing. Thursday Hale read her whole name off his list. She told him Lena. Saturday she ran the van to San Francisco. Six hours, row three. She asked me if I was happy. I said yes. At the end of the Walk I asked her how she had the nerve to be mad at me. She didn’t answer. She thanked me for coming and left.

s12b.slug: SATURDAY · 2:50 PM · THE END OF THE ROUTE — THE SAAB, AT THE CURB
body: The Saab comes up the Embarcadero against the buses with its top up and its hazards going, twenty-five minutes after she left in a cab to fetch it, and double-parks beside the van. The signs are going into the back in stacks.
His hands haven’t stopped shaking since the curb. He puts them in the pockets of the Carhartt, where they don’t show.

Skye looks at Jack’s face through the windshield. She puts the car in park, gets out, comes around the long hood with the hazards blinking orange on the both of them, and stands next to him on the curb with her shoulder against his arm, facing the way he’s facing, which is at nothing in particular.
Peter comes down the curb on his circuit, sees the Saab, sees Skye, and says “Ten past” to her too, politely, in case she’s coming.
“I’ll be ready,” Skye tells him, with a perfectly straight face, and Peter nods and moves on to Joey.

Kevin is in the van’s side door with the list against his chest and his pen uncapped. Behind him, through the open door, row three: the cooler in the aisle seat, Clare’s backpack of signs, the window and the middle.

Six hours either way. Six hours in a box with no door, with *Thank you for coming, Jack* sitting in the front of it, or six hours of the coast with the girl leaning on his arm. There isn’t a contest. There is Kevin, in a hall at half past eleven on Thursday in his pajama pants, asking him for something with an *I* in it.
“One second,” he tells Skye. She lets go of his arm.
He goes to the side door. “Kev. Can I ask you something, and you tell me the truth?”
“I always tell the truth. Margot says it’s a condition.”

“If I go back with Skye instead. Is that okay?” He keeps going before Kevin can be polite. “Because if you need me in the van the way you needed me to come up, I’ll get in the van. I mean it. I’ll sit on the cooler.”

Kevin looks at the list. He looks down the bench at Clare, who is in the second row with a rolled sign across her knees and her coat buttoned to the chin, talking to Becca. He looks at Jack’s face, and whatever is still on it from ten minutes ago, and Jack watches him take the question seriously, which is the only way Kevin knows how to take one.

“The brothers went home in Javi’s truck,” Kevin says. “Skye did the brothers. That was what I needed you for, and it’s done, and you didn’t even have to do it.” He clicks the pen. “So, the truth. I don’t need you. I’d like you. I sat next to Clare for six hours this morning and she was asleep for five of them. I don’t know what I talk about at hour four. That’s the truth. But that’s mine. You came. That was the ask.” He clicks the pen again. “Whichever. Really.”

s13s.slug: SATURDAY · 3:10–9:50 PM · US-101 SOUTH → PISMO BEACH, THE DUNES IN THE HEADLIGHTS
body: The Saab gets out of the city past the ballpark and up onto the freeway with the top up and the heater on their shins, and for the first twenty minutes neither of them says anything, and it’s fine.

South of the airport, with a plane coming in so low over the freeway he can read the tail, the clock on the dash turns over to 3:30. Skye looks at it, and then back at the road, and her hands move on the wheel to ten and two.

The Peninsula goes by, and San Jose, and the long flat stretch where the orchards used to be. At Gilroy the garlic comes in through the vents again, and she doesn’t make the joke. Her right thumb has started on the steering wheel, back and forth along the stitched seam at the top of it. He looks out at the outlet mall and lets it get where it’s going.
“My mother called Friday,” Skye says. “At seven. With notes.”
He waits.

“The cold on the *s*. She could hear the honey, she said; she always can. And the boathouse — she wanted the first *safe*, not the second. *You’re safe, sweetie.* She’d have hit the first one.” The thumb goes along the seam. “She’s right. I hate that she’s right. And then the coat. She said the peacoat was doing a lot of work, and somebody ought to tell craft services they weren’t helping it, and then she laughed, so it was a joke.” A truck goes by them on the right, loud. “I put her on speaker in the shower. I set the phone on the back of the toilet and turned the water up as far as it goes, so the water would be louder than she was. I stood in there forty minutes and said *uh-huh* every time she stopped.”
The thumb stops.
“I’m nineteen,” she says, “and I hide from my mother in a shower.”
He leaves it the size it is.

She’s bright again almost at once, too fast. “Anyway. I was very good in that boathouse. I’m a very good scene partner. Ask anybody — I give, I take, I listen, I land the button.” She checks the mirror, changes lanes, changes back. “I’m afraid I’m only a very good scene partner.”
He thinks of the curb an hour ago: the Saab double-parked with its hazards going and her getting out of it, coming around the hood, standing next to him facing nothing.
“Scene partners stay in the car,” he says.

She looks over at him, fast, and back at the road, and something goes out of her shoulders. “That’s a good note,” she says. “I’m stealing it.” Then: “Your turn. I went first. That’s how it works — I go first, and then you have somewhere to put yours.”
There was a fight, he tells her. At the van, after she left for the car.
“About?”
“About you,” he says. “Sort of.”
He hears how small that is as soon as it’s out. She hears it too; her thumb doesn’t start again. There’s a name in the car and nobody says it.
“There’s more,” he says. “There’s Tuesday too. I’m going to tell you. Not in the dark at seventy, with you driving.”
She keeps her eyes on the road a long moment. “Daylight,” she says, the way she’d write it on a call sheet, and lets it be.

South of Salinas the light goes. The fields on both sides turn blue, and then there are only the long silver lines of the irrigation pipe holding on to the last of it, and then not even those. She reaches over and thumbs through the iPod in the cupholder and puts something on — a guitar, two voices, low and close and hardly there — in place of the next question.

At King City she gets off for gas and goes in to buy, she announces, the worst snacks in the store, on principle. Under the canopy lights he turns on the RAZR, which has been off in the Carhartt since the curb, and it buzzes four times at once against his palm, everything two hours old, the way it does when it comes back from nowhere.

body: She comes back out with a plastic bag — pork rinds, circus peanuts, a Big Hunk, a pickle in a pouch — and gets in, and he reads her the third one.
“What’s the Dell?”
“The computer. In the kitchen, by the phone.” He can see it. “She doesn’t sit down at it. She stands over it with her arms folded, like it might be catching.”
Skye sits with the bag in her lap and the key in her hand, looking at the pumps. Then she starts the car.

By San Ardo she has recovered enough to present the snacks. She holds each one up into the dash light and scores it out of ten for badness — the pork rinds a solid six, the pickle an eight “for the pouch alone,” the Big Hunk a mystery she refuses to score until she’s chewed it for a full minute. He tells her circus peanuts are illegal in Ohio. She makes him eat one. It tastes like a banana that went to the dentist, and he says so, and she laughs so hard she drifts onto the rumble strip and back.

Somewhere past Paso Robles he tells her he’s going to meet the van at midnight at St. Brendan’s and help Kevin with the signs. He doesn’t tell her the other half of why. She says it’s very Catholic of him, and it comes out kind.

Past San Luis Obispo she takes the exit for the beach without a word. She goes down Grand Avenue to where the road runs out onto the sand — a ramp for trucks, a sign about the tide, no other car — and stops at the foot of it with the headlights out across the dunes to the water, where the surf stands up white in the beams and falls over.

She cuts the engine and leaves the lights on. She’s out of her shoes and out of the car before he has his seat belt off, running down the sand into the headlights in her jeans, and she doesn’t stop at the edge. She goes straight into the Pacific in January, to her knees, to her waist, and a wave stands up in the light and comes down on top of her, and she comes up out of it shrieking.
“*No people!*” she shouts back at him, arms out. “*There aren’t any people!*”

He shrugs the Carhartt off onto the seat and goes in after her. The cold doesn’t feel like cold; it feels like being hit. It takes the breath out of him in one piece and his whole body locks up around his heart, and she’s laughing at him with her teeth going, and the next wave takes the two of them down together, and when he comes up he’s wet to the skin and past it, salt in his nose and his ears, and she has him by the front of the Mooney hoodie and kisses him with her mouth cold and tasting of the sea. Up and down the beach, as far as the headlights go, the sand is empty. He is laughing too.

Walking back up the sand to the car, dripping, her shoes in one hand and his wrist in the other, she says it again, quieter. “Thirty-five thousand people today. And nobody wanted anything from me. Not one.” She lets go of his wrist to push the wet hair off her face. “I didn’t know where to put my face. All day. I kept waiting for somebody to need it.”
He takes the shoes from her, so she has both hands for her hair.

Afterward they sit in the Saab with the doors shut and the heater on full and the headlights still out over the water, steaming like two pots on a stove. Her hair hangs in black strings. His jeans weigh forty pounds.

She doesn’t stay on her side of the car for long. She comes across the console with the salt still running out of her hair, cold everywhere he touches and hot everywhere he doesn’t, and inside a minute the windows have gone white all the way around, the headlights blooming in the fog on the glass. His hands are under the wet shirt at the small of her back and hers are inside the soaked hoodie, flat on his ribs, and the seat lever gives under somebody’s knee and lays him halfway back with her on top of him. Yesterday afternoon was all daylight, and he knew where every step of it was. Tonight there is a dark beach and a blind car and the nearest other headlights miles off, and somewhere in it he stops keeping count. He doesn’t notice when. It’s the gearshift that brings him back: the knob in her hip, her yelp into his mouth. He gets a hand on the dash and hauls the seat back up. His hands are shaking, and it isn’t the water. She looks at him from very close in the green light, breathing hard. Then she climbs back to her side and turns the heater up a notch it doesn’t have.

When they have their breath back she digs the white phone out of the glove box, where she left it safe, holds it out at arm’s length with the back toward them, leans her soaked head against his, and takes it. She turns it around to look: two drowned people in a car, lit green from below by the dashboard with the black windshield behind, her mouth open laughing and his eyes shut against her hair.

s13v.slug: SATURDAY · 3:10–11:50 PM · US-101 SOUTH — THE BACK BENCH
body: The van pulls away from the curb at the end of the route at ten past three with the signs stacked flat in the back like a deck of very large cards, and the low sun slides down the cross streets at it, and Peter takes the ramp with both hands and a rosary swinging from the mirror.

Lena is on the front bench beside him. She and Kenzie traded places at the curb, and nobody remarked on it; Kenzie, who rode up shotgun with an atlas she didn’t need, was out of the front seat before the sentence was over. She is now in row three at Jack’s shoulder, shining, with the road atlas in her lap and her BlackBerry in her fist.
“Okay, I’m not going to be weird,” she says. “Is she nice? Like nice nice, or TV nice?”
“She ranked four brothers by height out loud.”
“That’s *TV* nice,” Kenzie breathes, in awe.
“Kenzie. She didn’t want anything posted.”

The shine goes off her all at once. She is twenty, and a cantor, and her face was built to be read from the back of a church. “Oh,” she says. “Oh, no. I thought — she stood in front of Clare. I just wanted people to know she was *good*.”
“She is.” It is true, and it is the problem, and he can’t think how to say both halves to a girl holding a BlackBerry like a hymnal. “Leave it up. It’s done.”
Kenzie nods several times. “Can I still ask you something and you won’t get mad?”
“No.”
From the back bench, a hand goes up, white, with a thermos in it. “Costigan,” says Margot. “The back bench has a window and no follow-up questions.”
He is over the cooler and into the last row before Kenzie has finished saying, “Wait, I have *so* many,” and the van slides onto the freeway and sets itself south.

South of the city, with the planes coming in low over the freeway toward the airport, he takes the RAZR out of the Carhartt and turns it on long enough for the little screen to say 3:30, and turns it off again before anything can come in. It goes back in the pocket and stays there.
Margot sits beside him with the notebook shut on her knee and the pen capped. She has said nothing for twenty minutes. When she speaks, she keeps her eyes on the Peninsula.

body.text: “You said ‘any of this.’ I wrote down ‘this.’”
body.else: “I didn’t hear what you said to her at the curb,” she says. “I saw her hands.”

body: He looks at the notebook, and then at the side of her face. She doesn’t say anything else, and from Margot that is a mercy. After a while he takes the Ziploc out of the Carhartt and holds it open between them, and Margot inspects the pair and takes the one on the left.
“Peanut butter,” she says. “No jelly.”
“The Commons was out.”
“Then it’s honest.” She eats it in four bites, looking out at the long gray shopping centers, and what she says when it’s gone is, “Acceptable.”
Past Gilroy the garlic comes in through the vents, and Joey identifies it, loudly, by name.
“They make garlic ice cream,” Tyler says, with a missionary’s awe.
“That isn’t a sin,” says Bridget. “It’s a crime.”

By Salinas the light is gone, the lettuce fields are black on both sides, and the windows have turned to mirrors. Kevin and Clare have moved back to row four, nearer the signs, and Kevin has been working up to it since the city; he swivels all the way around in his seat.
“Okay. Before the brothers.” He actually stops. “You didn’t have to ride with us. I know the other car was right there.”
“I said I would.”

“I know you did. I’m saying I know.” It lasts exactly as long as he can stand it. “So, the brothers.” He has the clipboard against his chest, a shield. “Javi, the oldest, asked my intentions. In front of the *Ferry Building*. I said ‘Honorable, sir,’ and he said ‘I’m twenty-seven, don’t call me sir,’ and Luis put me in a headlock, which Clare says is how they say they like you, and Nico asked to see my hands —”
“Your hands.”

“They’re all very hands. Tito didn’t say a word and shook mine for what I’d estimate was nine seconds. And your girlfriend asked Javi one question about Montana, and he has never been so happy in his life.” He drops his voice, which does nothing, because Clare is beside him, and Clare is not fooled. “And Javi said I can come to a Niners game. *The* Niners. At the actual stadium, with the family.”
“It’s a very good stadium,” Clare says. “It’s a bad team.” She is nineteen, with a violinist’s calluses on her left hand, and she hasn’t said much since the man with the megaphone.
Jack leans forward over the seat back. “Kev. Is a march a date?”
Kevin doesn’t say anything fast. “It was,” he says.
Clare says nothing. She turns her face to the window, where there is nothing now but the lit inside of the van and a valley behind it, and keeps it there.

Peter stops at the King City Burger King at twenty to seven, because the route says so and because Joey has begun to chant. The Burger King is lit like an operating room. The teenager at the register says, “Welcome to Burger King,” to fourteen people who have been looking at one another since five in the morning.

In the lot, under the sign, Jack turns the RAZR on for the first time since the freeway, and it takes a minute to remember where it is, and then it delivers everything at once. Four texts from Gina, stamped with the hours they were sent, nearly three hours back.

He can see where it landed: the Dell on the kitchen table, and his mother standing over it with her arms folded instead of sitting down, because sitting would mean she was staying. *That’s something.* It is not the sentence he was braced for. Peter’s route gives King City thirty minutes and the word DINNER in bold. “I’m not going to ask,” she tells Jack. “I’m going to tell you I’ve been praying since San Francisco, and I’m not going to say who for. It’s a lot of people for one van. I’ve been doing it in shifts.”

Joey, at the end of the line, has his phone held out at arm’s length like a lantern. He has been following the Cavs for Jack since the lot, on the theory that Ohio is Ohio, and Jack grew up in a house that has suffered for Cleveland since before he was born; this winter the one Cleveland thing that isn’t suffering is a man from Akron.
“GIBSON!” Joey says. The whole restaurant looks up from its fries. “GIBSON! A HUNDRED TO NINETY-NINE! HE HIT THE THREE!”
“Congratulations?” says the teenager at the register.

Jack finds he is on his feet in the middle of a Burger King with his hand in Joey Abruzzo’s, pumping it, and Tyler has started on a chant that has no words, and at the booth by the window Peter has the laminated route out between the trays. Lena is across from him with her finger on a line of it. She looks up, with everyone, at the noise. She looks down.

Peter counts heads in the lot, twice, and gets fourteen, the right number, and they go back out into the dark with the radio low, a ranchera from a station in Salinas, and Peter humming the parts he knows.

South of Atascadero the van tops the rise above the Cuesta Grade and finds the whole southbound side stopped below it, a long red river of taillights going down into the dark: a big rig over on its side across two lanes near the bottom, flares in a line, a CHP cruiser turning its lights around and around on the rock. They sit there an hour and ten minutes with the engine off and the heater going cold. Peter leads a decade for the driver. Joey eats the last of everybody’s fries. Kenzie falls asleep on the atlas.
Somewhere ahead of them on the same road the Saab is going south with its top up and one person in it.

s14.slug: SUNDAY · 12:10 AM · ST. BRENDAN’S LOT — THE VAN COMES HOME

body.text: The van turns in off Ocean Road and rocks to a stop under the lot’s one sodium light, where it stood at five this morning with its side door open and everybody’s breath showing. The door rolls back. He gets out last, behind the signs.

He walked down from Delgado at a quarter to twelve. He’s at the edge of the lot with his hands in the Carhartt, in dry jeans, his hair still stiff with salt, when the van turns in off Ocean Road and rocks to a stop under the sodium light, where it stood at five this morning with everybody’s breath showing.

body: They come off it like people who have been nine hours in a van. Joey, asleep on his feet, steered by the elbow. Becca with the long red knitting rolled under her arm, lifting a hand to Jack as she passes. Peter, stiff, unlocking the hall with a ring of keys the size of a saucer.

Lena comes down off the front step with the clipboard against her chest and starts across the lot toward Ocean Road, toward Delgado, and he’s standing in the way of it. She doesn’t go around him. She goes past, near enough that he hears the clip of the clipboard tick against a button on her peacoat, and she doesn’t look at him, and he doesn’t say her name. The van’s brakes tick as they cool.

At the side door Kevin says goodnight to Clare. He puts his hand out and she takes it, and they shake, up and down, and it goes on past where a handshake ends, and neither of them seems to know what comes next. Kevin’s ears go red under the sodium light. “Night, Kevin,” Clare says, and shoulders the backpack of signs, and crosses the lot toward the dorms.

Jack carries signs into the hall for Kevin until there aren’t any. When he comes back out for the cooler, Kevin and Peter are arguing in whispers over the clipboard about whether a sign is missing, and he goes and sits on the low wall by the side door, under the olive tree, to wait.

It’s waiting for him there. It starts in his fingers, which want something to do; then in his mouth, the taste of it arriving ahead of the thing. His own pack is in the inside pocket of the Carhartt, with the lighter. The tin is in the other pocket, and it isn’t his.
The last one was Wednesday’s, in the roof door at Delgado with the rain coming in on his knees.
The olive tree moves a little over him. Across the courtyard a light is on in the rectory, upstairs. His hand is inside the jacket.
